answers.What is your top issue this year?: In my opinion the single most important issue facing New Jersey today is preserving our state’s rights. I say this in the face of a federal administration that is looking to take away our rights.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: To make NJ more affordable, I support the following:
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: To address housing affordability, I would support legislation requiring municipalities to abide by the Mt. Laurel Doctrine, considered to be one of the strongest frameworks in the country to prevent and address residential segregation. The Mt. Lauren Doctrine outlawed exclusionary zoning and required a “Fair Share” of all developments to be affordable based on a municipality’s regional need for housing (at least 13%). Originally, the Council on Affordable Housing (COAH) oversaw compliance but was removed from the statute. I would push to reinstate COAH. I would also support legislation to allow Accessory Dwelling Units (ADUs) in NJ. ADUs are independent living spaces built on the same lot as a single-family home.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: To protect programs that traditionally received federal funding but may not under Trump, I plan to introduce legislation to protect NJ State Rights. The legislation will allow NJ to funnel federal income tax withheld from NJ Residents’ paychecks into a NJ State Trust Fund. Any expenses the state incurs as a direct result of federal cuts will be paid out of the NJ State Trust Fund. At the end of the fiscal year, any remaining money in the NJ State Trust Fund will be sent to the federal government. As a state, NJ has aways paid more in federal tax dollars then it has received back in services from the federal government. We have accepted that inequity for years but cannot accept an additional cut in services because the president is a racist.

answers.Occupation: Chief Executive Officer, Ranch Hope Inc.
answers.Personal or professional background: It’s an honor to serve as State Assemblyman for New Jersey’s Third Legislative District, building on my lifelong commitment to serving children, youth, and families. As CEO of Ranch Hope, a faith-based nonprofit, I lead 200 dedicated staff supporting vulnerable youth across South Jersey. With over 30 years of experience, I’ve worked across government and community sectors to advocate for policies that make a difference. I hold a master’s in nonprofit management from Eastern University, volunteer with Meals on Wheels, and am a proud member of the Rotary Club of Woodstown. My wife Julie and I live in Woodstown and have three adult children.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: Our state is facing an affordability crisis that’s hitting families especially hard. From rising property taxes and utility bills to healthcare, childcare, and groceries, the cost of living is stretching household budgets thin. We must hold the line on taxes, deliver the promised 50% property tax cut for seniors, and expand relief for working families. I support limiting utility rate hikes, increasing energy production, and investing in rural communities through agriculture, transportation, and small business support. My focus is on fighting for South Jersey to get its fair share—and for government to make life more affordable for everyone.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: South Jersey is in the grip of an affordability crisis that’s straining household budgets and holding back our economy. From rising property taxes to utility bills, groceries, and healthcare, working families are being squeezed. Tackling this requires real action—capping utility rate hikes, delivering tax relief for seniors, and investing in rural communities. That means supporting family farms, expanding high-speed internet, and growing local businesses. A stronger, more affordable South Jersey starts with a fair economy that works for everyone—not just a few. We must ensure our region gets its fair share and the tools needed to thrive.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: Affordable housing is a vital part of addressing New Jersey’s affordability crisis, especially for young people looking to build their future here. We must support first-time homebuyers, veterans, and working families without compromising the character, history, or tourism that define our communities. Thoughtful, well-planned development can expand housing options while preserving what makes our towns unique. By doing so, we strengthen local economies, support schools and small businesses, and give more families the opportunity to put down roots and thrive.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: New Jersey’s rising state budget and looming federal cuts to healthcare and education put our most vulnerable communities at risk—especially in rural South Jersey, where healthcare deserts already exist. I support a fiscally responsible approach that lowers taxes, reins in spending, and ensures every dollar is used wisely. With one of the lowest returns on the tax dollars we send to Washington, we must fight back against unfair federal cuts that threaten hospitals, clinics, and patient care. By focusing on smart, efficient spending, we can protect essential services, support rural communities, and make life more affordable for all New Jerseyans.

answers.Personal or professional background: Chris Konawel is a lifelong South Jersey resident, raised in South Harrison Township and now living in Glassboro. answers.What is your top issue this year?: I am committed to addressing the fiscal crisis facing our community by cutting wasteful spending and ensuring tax relief for working families. I will focus on transparency and accountability, and make sure residents know how their tax dollars are used. I will immediately work to resolve school funding disparities that disproportionately affect south Jersey and tackle the insane utility bills that are putting financial strain on families. I am an advocate for small business, i support policies that foster economic growth and job creation. I will always stand with law enforcement to keep communities safe, and lead with ethical, principled decisions.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: New Jersey’s fiscal health has been strained for years, burdened by excessive debt, unsustainable spending, and an over-reliance on temporary financial fixes. The state’s budget is too often marked by inefficiencies, high borrowing, and rising taxes, creating an environment where middle-class families and businesses bear the brunt. To achieve long-term economic stability and make New Jersey more affordable for residents, a comprehensive fiscal responsibility and budget reform plan is essential.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: New Jersey residents are burdened by some of the highest housing costs in the nation, including expensive rents and skyrocketing property taxes. While increasing the stock of low-income housing is a solution some advocate for, I believe there are other ways to reduce housing costs without mandating additional low-income housing. Through zoning reforms, incentivizing affordable housing development, reducing property taxes, and supporting first-time homebuyers, we can significantly lower housing costs for all New Jersey residents.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: Managing healthcare/social services/education cuts due to reductions in federal support is an immense challenge for any state. New Jersey, in particular, faces significant pressure to continue providing essential services despite these challenges. The key to successfully managing funding cuts lies in a combination of strategic use of state resources, promoting efficiency, and pursuing innovative solutions.

answers.Occupation: Vice President, Workforce Innovation and Partnerships – Rowan College of South Jersey
answers.Personal or professional background: I’m running for reelection because South Jersey families deserve real solutions—not soundbites—on rising costs, healthcare, and opportunity for the next generation. answers.What is your top issue this year?: Affordability is the most pressing issue facing our families, from rising utility bills to grocery cost and property taxes. I also passed a bipartisan law targeting organized retail theft. In a divided climate, I’ve proven we can still work together. I’m committed to practical solutions—expanding workforce training, improving education and healthcare access, and ensuring South Jersey gets its fair share—so families aren’t punished just for getting sick.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: Rising costs—from utilities to groceries—are straining New Jersey families. I introduced the Electric Bill Cap Act to limit utility rate hikes for households earning up to $120,000 and sponsored grants to help small businesses impacted by public construction. I’m committed to practical, fiscally responsible solutions: expanding workforce training, improving healthcare access, and ensuring South Jersey gets its fair share. My priority is making our communities more affordable and supporting working families with policies that deliver real, lasting relief.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: Affordable housing is a critical part of addressing New Jersey’s affordability crisis. We must support first-time homebuyers, veterans, and working families so they can live in safe, welcoming communities of their choice. That means expanding housing options through strong partnerships with municipalities and by leveraging state and federal resources to meet local needs. Expanding housing options in a way that aligns with local planning strengthens our economy, supports schools and small businesses, and helps families put down roots.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: I believe in a fiscally responsible approach to government that lowers taxes, reduces wasteful spending, and protects New Jersey taxpayers. Our state already receives one of the lowest returns on the dollars we send to Washington, and I’m standing up to harmful federal cuts that threaten essential services. By prioritizing smart budgeting and efficient use of resources, we can ease the burden on working families while investing in the services our communities rely on. New Jersey taxpayers deserve fairness and accountability—both in Trenton and in Washington.

This directory would include key details like availability, application instructions, and whether a property has a waitlist, making it easier for residents to find and apply for housing. With better information and coordination, we can create a more efficient, transparent, and equitable housing system for all New Jerseyans.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: I advocate for a fiscally responsible approach to governance that reduces taxes, eliminates wasteful spending, and protects taxpayers in New Jersey. Our state consistently receives one of the lowest returns on the federal dollars we contribute, and I am committed to opposing harmful federal cuts that threaten vital services. With smart budgeting and efficient resource use, we can relieve the financial burden on working families while continuing to invest in the essential programs our communities depend on. Taxpayers deserve fairness and accountability in Trenton and Washington.

answers.Personal or professional background: A dedicated troubleshooter and problem-solver, Spearman is widely recognized across New Jersey for his commitment to public service. answers.What is your top issue this year?: Affordability for NJ residents.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: My top priority is making NJ affordable. We have the StayNJ property tax relief program in place, which will provide significant property tax reductions for seniors, cutting taxes in half starting in January 2026. I have dedicated the past two years to ensuring this initiative delivers meaningful, long-term relief. If you need help with your application, my office is always available. Additionally, we are currently holding hearings to address utility companies planning to raise rates this summer while continuing to report record profits. This is unacceptable, and I am committed to holding these companies accountable.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: I support making housing more affordable in New Jersey. We passed a law that will create 85,000 new homes across the state, helping to lower costs for families looking to buy a house. Additionally, we’ve allocated millions of dollars to first-time homebuyer programs to assist with down payments. While I’m proud of these efforts, I know they’re just the beginning. We’re also offering incentives to municipalities to build more housing near transit centers, which will drive down costs and make living here more affordable for everyone.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: I am committed to protecting and prioritizing these vital programs. I’ve supported budgets that have significantly increased funding for these services. Under Gov. Murphy’s, for every dollar spent on K-12 public education when he took office, we now spend $1.50, with additional investments in pre-K, college, community colleges, and apprenticeship programs. Despite challenges posed by federal cuts, we’ve been able to make historic investments in critical areas. I am confident that by focusing on healthcare, education, and services, and providing meaningful property tax relief for our residents, we will continue to protect these essential services and strengthen New Jersey’s future.

answers.What is your top issue this year?: We need to implement an improved Medicare for All New Jersey residents. People can’t get the care they need, are going into debt and losing their homes as a result of medical expenses, and they can’t get the often life-saving care they need. The way to offset people being kicked off of Medicaid, is to guarantee that all residents of New Jersey get their medical expenses covered, regardless of income.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: Medicare for All will eliminate tremendous expenses for health insurance premiums for both patients and their employers. We need to provide housing subsidies for most NJ residents, guaranteeing everyone will have a place to live, and will be able to afford their other expenses – food, clothing, transportation, utilities, etc.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: I support laws designed to increase affordable housing, including rent control laws that would put caps on rent increases. Senior citizens should be able to live in their houses, free of property taxes, and we must provide housing and counseling for homeless individuals, to help them get out of poverty.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: Once again, Medicare for All NJ residents would eliminate the need for Medicaid. Instead of sending money to Israel, as New Jersey does, that money could be earmarked for education, especially to hire more teachers to eliminate overcrowding in classrooms, and assure students more one-on-one attention. We also need to increase taxes on millionaires and billionaires, closing loopholes used to avoid paying taxes at all. The revenue from an increased wealth tax could provide funding for food assistance, social services, housing subsidies, etc.

answers.Personal or professional background: I am a lifelong resident of the 6th Legislative District and have proudly represented it in the Assembly since 1996. As Majority Leader I bring not just legislative experience, but the values I learned from my mother, Maria Barnaby Greenwald, the first female mayor of Cherry Hill. I draw great inspiration from my mom, using her lessons of tireless advocacy and thoughtful consideration of issues to guide my work representing the people of the 6th District.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: New Jersey is on the right track, but the main issue that we continue to deal with is affordability in the state. People continue to see their property taxes go up as they pay more to stay in towns they’ve long called home. Healthcare remains a massive issue for our state, with people paying more and more for coverage that covers less and less. We also see housing becoming more and more unaffordable, with a severe lack of workforce housing in our state contributing to young professionals choosing to leave New Jersey at an alarming rate. It’s become harder to call New Jersey home, and I am committed to helping fix that.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: Increasing affordability begins with tackling the costs that hit our families the hardest. Property taxes are a top issue in the state, and I am proud of my work in creating the ANCHOR, Senior Freeze, and StayNJ property tax relief programs that put money back into our taxpayer’s pockets. I am committed to fully funding these programs so people in our state can get the relief they deserve. In healthcare, rising prices are a growing burden. I’ve sponsored legislation like A5217 to take on the middlemen driving up prescription costs, and I’ll continue pushing for reforms that hold drug companies accountable and lower costs for everyday New Jerseyans.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: New Jersey is suffering from a brain drain; young professionals who studied in our state and call New Jersey home are leaving because housing costs and rents have skyrocketed. We must make housing more affordable by changing oppressive zoning laws that overly incentivize houses far too large to be affordable for the average person. By allowing development, we can bring down the costs for young families to stay in New Jersey and live where they have long called home.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: New Jersey already receives the lowest return on investment from the federal government, we send more than we get back. I’m committed to holding our federal representatives accountable to ensure New Jersey gets a fair deal, especially with these proposed harmful cuts to essential services our state relies on. I’ve spoken out against these proposals on the Assembly floor, and I will continue to forcefully oppose any action that threatens our communities.

answers.Personal or professional background: I am a retired IBM Delivery Project Executive and former public school educator running as a Republican for New Jersey’s 6th Legislative District Assembly. My professional background bridges the private and public sectors, with leadership experience in global business application development and classroom instruction. I began my career teaching in the Cinnaminson, Washington Township, and Camden school districts, gaining firsthand insight into the challenges facing our education system. I bring both business acumen and educational experience to the legislative table.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: After 20 years of uninterrupted Democrat governance, New Jersey ranks among the worst in the nation for property taxes, corporate tax burdens, and housing affordability. Despite a record-high state budget, we remain mired in a structural deficit—proof of unsustainable, unchecked spending. Our student learning standards are, by law, infused with DEI ideology, gender ideology, and “keeping secrets from parents” policies in K-12. This undermines both academic rigor and parental rights and will come to an end. We will terminate sanctuary state policies, end the offshore wind boondoggle, reinstate voter ID, and eliminate cashless bail.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: Put Jersey Families FIRST.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: The current affordable housing mandate, rooted in the Mt. Laurel court ruling, was never passed by the legislature, never debated, and never subjected to a vote. No elected official was held accountable—nor did Jersey voters vote on this. Yet today, our most cherished towns face state lawsuits and “builder’s remedy” schemes forcing high-density housing into small communities unequipped for urban-scale development. It’s time to reject this judicial overreach. We must prioritize pathways for young families to access existing single-family homes and expand homeownership opportunities—not pave over our neighborhoods with dense housing blocks. Revitalize communities, don’t erase them. Restore legislative control. Build responsibly.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: During COVID, the federal government let millions stay on Medicaid, even if they no longer qualified. Now that the emergency rules are over, it turns out many of the people being cut weren’t eligible in the first place. Some aren’t U.S. citizens. Others can work and should be encouraged to do so. New Jersey shouldn’t spend state tax dollars to keep ineligible people on Medicaid. Help should go to those who truly need it—our seniors, disabled, and struggling families. We need to bring fairness, common sense, and responsibility back to how we handle public assistance.The cuts were aimed at non-citizens and able-bodied individuals. Non-citizens should be repatriated, and the others should go back to work.

answers.Personal or professional background: I’m a longtime Camden County resident, a Gold Star Mother, public servant, and passionate advocate for veterans and military families. With a background in education, social work, and small business, I’ve had the honor of serving as a Cherry Hill councilwoman, Camden County Commissioner, and now as a member of the New Jersey General Assembly representing the 6th District. My work is driven by a deep commitment to community, compassion, and public service.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: As a legislator, I hear every day from constituents who are struggling with the burden of high property taxes—it’s why property tax relief remains my top priority. Programs like StayNJ are critical tools in addressing this challenge and making New Jersey more affordable, especially for seniors. StayNJ provides significant relief by reimbursing eligible older homeowners for up to 50% of their property tax bills, helping them stay in their homes and communities. By streamlining and expanding access to existing relief programs, we’re taking meaningful steps to ease the financial strain and ensure a more secure future for all residents.

answers.Personal or professional background: I live in Union County with my wife and our two little kids. I went to the same NJ public schools my mom did, and they helped me get to Harvard Law School. I served as a federal and state prosecutor in Newark and Jersey City, prosecuting crimes from gun trafficking to fraud that stole millions from COVID relief funds. Then I worked as counsel to the state AG, and started a program that pairs police with mental health workers to respond jointly to crisis 911 calls and is now operating in dozens of towns across NJ.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: NJ Transit. Public transportation is a basic government function. It is vital to our economy, commutes, and to environmental efforts. NJT is the third largest public transit system in the country, yet it continues to disappoint. We need champions at all levels of government who will make sure a new Hudson River tunnel is built, and who will put forward pragmatic solutions to improve service while that work is being done: 1) providing real-time, accurate train location data, 2) bringing new rail cars online that were ordered 8 years ago, 3) ensuring Amtrak accelerates infrastructure repairs as promised.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: Work towards the root causes of rising costs, not just band-aids on the problem. Property taxes – find practical methods of sharing services and cutting down redundancies like coordinating contract negotiations across towns. Childcare – support providers in entering the market to increase options and lower costs. Energy prices – in the short term increase supply through creative solutions like connecting ready-to-go power plants to underutilized existing grid connections, and in the long term pursue diversified sources of supply that are as cost-effective, efficient, and renewable as possible.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: The housing law’s formula that mandates a number of units to build fails to reflect the realities of many towns. Too much focus has been placed on building many market rate units to subsidize a few “affordable” ones. Puzzlingly, developers are allowed to sue municipalities for not building enough. This all can lead to unsustainable development in places like my district. Housing should be built in a bespoke manner—in consultation with professional planners—that fits amongst existing structures in a community. And the approval process for state funds available for towns seeking to build workforce housing should be streamlined.
answers.How would you manage federal funding cut: Bring lawsuits against the federal government where appropriate. Make our state budget as efficient and effective as possible, including by requiring long-term budget forecasting in order to confront the ongoing structural deficit. Prioritize use of the current surplus as best we can to plug the worst holes left by federal cuts in a sustainable manner. And, at the end of the day, organize and elect better federal representatives.

answers.Occupation: Detective for the Union County Sheriff’s Department
answers.Personal or professional background: I’m a husband and father of twin boys, a Union County Sheriff’s Detective, and a Councilman in Garwood Borough. I’ve managed tight budgets at home, on the job, and on the Council. I plan to take my lifelong experience in public service to Trenton to fight for our community and make New Jersey a safer and more affordable place to live for everyone.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: My top priority is making New Jersey work better for us.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: I want to restore the full amount of Energy Tax Receipts collected by the state government to the municipal level. Decades ago, the state rebranded this as “state aid,” and not only do our towns get pennies on the dollar, but we often have to fight to get that. Restoration would enable local governments to better control property taxes at the source.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: I agree that we need more affordable housing in New Jersey, but I do not support the current law as it stands. This issue cannot be solved by exclusively building in large cities or ending all development. Instead, we need to coordinate development across the state and leverage existing systems to encourage the building of a diverse range of housing types; we need housing that is both affordable and suitable for first-time homebuyers. Affordable housing laws must evolve to better protect municipalities from large developers, who push projects larger than necessary to maximize their profits with high rents that leave people out in the cold. Further, we should crack down on predatory lenders and landlords who manipulate rates and rents.
answers.How would you manage federal funding cut: We have a moral obligation to ensure that destructive federal cuts to services such as public education, Medicaid, Social Security, reproductive healthcare clinics, mental health support, transit, and flood mitigation projects, are offset. As a state representative, I will advocate for restoring and improving the federal services our tax dollars pay for, while doing everything in my power to support candidates for federal office who will do the same so that we don’t have to bear the burden of funding these alone. I will also work with my colleagues to ensure our state budget surplus is used wisely. I will go line-by-line in each budget, just as I have both at home and as a Councilman, to cut wasteful spending and review existing programs.

answers.Personal or professional background: I started a multimillion dollar company in South Korea when I was in my twenties. I returned home to take care of my mother, who had brain cancer. I got involved in politics around then when I first ran for office in 2023, having realized that my industrial organizational skills were applicable. I am good, for example, at solving problems, networking, connecting with people about their needs, and representing them.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: I have three top issues. First, we need to stop the overdevelopment of warehouses. These are being turned into fulfillment centers, AI data centers, and worst of all – potentially illegally-operating ICE detention facilities. Instead we need preserve farmland, and renew, and redevelop the empty buildings that we already have, for purposes that better suit heritage tourism and main street businesses. Second, we need to emphasize the trades and occupational skills more in public schools, supporting apprenticeships and union membership. Third, we need to cut the red tape holding back small businesses, entrepreneurs, and working professionals from making money.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: My running mate Tyler Powell talks about this all the time, and he is far more intelligent on the subject than I, but I agree with him that we need to localize our power supply with micro grids to offset the skyrocketing costs of energy. There is no reason why, for example, our energy prices are surging, when we can put more solar panels on top of municipal buildings, other publicly owned spaces, and over parking lots, to generate and profit from power, locally. Furthermore, that would create all kinds of opportunities and jobs for technical, skilled, and union workforces, again, locally. I’ll speak more on housing affordability in the next section.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: I think we need to end the corporate ownership of single family dwellings, and residential buildings. BlackRock, for example, should not be allowed in the housing investment market because they are clearly speculating, and causing prices to rise artificially. Property values, instead, should come from local quality of life improvements and other types of community investments like in our school systems, and infrastructure. To increase supply, we also need to encourage our boroughs and cities that can – to build affordable housing. Confronting the “builder’s remedy” issue in the Mount Laurel Agreement will be important on that front.
answers.How would you manage federal funding cut: I believe we have to tax the top 1% and top performing companies, specifically in the insurance sectors, more, in a manner that is equitable. So, exactly “how” is a discussion we should have publicly, often, and work with stakeholders across the board to achieve. We also need a more long-term strategy for how to deal with the fact that we are a net-donor state, in terms of federal taxation, meaning that we were not receiving enough federal service as it was the case even before the Budget Reconciliation Bill of 2025. I don’t, for example, understand why our hard-earned dollars are going to “Red States” – to fund and supplement their operations – while their legislators are voting to cut our essential services.

answers.Plain: Age: 35 years old Hometown: Franklin Twp (Hunterdon) Occupation: Cybersecurity Professional Personal or professional background: I grew up in Texas around horses and cowboys, and spent my childhood helping out at my family’s grocery store. I was a childhood epileptic. In my early 20s, I fell on hard times and lived out of my truck for a while. I then moved to New Jersey and started my life over. I put myself through RVCC and got my bachelor’s degree from Rutgers in Management and Labor Relations. I currently work in cybersecurity, defending critical infrastructure. What is your top issue this year? New Jersey lacks a real energy policy. With the way rates are spiking, we need a new path forward to manage electricity costs and ensure New Jersey’s energy independence while meeting climate goals. Ben Franklin once described New Jersey as “a keg tapped at both ends.” I say we make NJ a battery tapped at both ends, exporting power to New York and Philadelphia instead. We need smaller grids that are locally controlled, and the option for municipalities and counties to create their own coops. What are your specific proposals for making New Jersey more affordable? There’s no quick fix. Invest heavily into new clean energy production to create good jobs and stabilize the cost of electricity for residents. Build more housing (in the right places) and ban corporate ownership to help ease the pressure from the extreme demand we’re seeing across the country. Property taxes are some of the highest in the nation, and to reduce costs without cutting services, we must turn to economies of scale. Not necessarily consolidation, but move services to county or state operation. We can’t keep looking at issues through the lens of our individual fiefdoms, arguing over which level of government should pay for what. We must do what is most efficient, where it leads to gains in quality of life across our state. Do you support the state law designed to increase the amount of affordable housing, and if not, how would you make housing less costly for residents? I’m in favor of more affordable housing, but it doesn’t make sense to put it in the middle of nowhere. Tell me why Union Twp should have to build 300 units of affordable housing off the side of I-78. It’s absurd. You get all the downside of apartment living and none of the upside. There’s plenty of opportunities to build housing in already denser, walkable areas with public transit and the State should do everything in its power to make sure affordable housing gets built there. I support community revitalization funding and planning that works to strengthen downtowns across NJ’s unique communities. We should make the places people already want to live better and repurpose already developed spaces, not sacrifice farmland for development. How should the state deal with federal funding cuts to Medicaid, food assistance, education and other areas? We’ll need to fund it ourselves. Taxing the top 1% and large cap corporations (especially with the giant handout they’ve just been given by the BBB) will allow us to take care of New Jerseyans and the people of LD23 who need it the most until we can take back the federal government. Find more information

answers.Personal or professional background: My career in education began as a teacher, later serving as principal and district administrator, with experience in both traditional public and public charter schools. I served three years on the Franklin Borough Council, including as Council President, and five years as a Sussex County Commissioner (Freeholder), including time as Director, where I prioritized the needs of rural northwest New Jersey. I am now a Republican Assemblywoman serving on the Education Committee, the Commerce, Economic Development & Agriculture Committee, and the Aging & Human Services Committee, as well as the GOP Energy Task Force. As the mother of three, I bring both professional and personal perspective to advocating for working families and rural communities.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: My top issue this election is restoring true affordability by tackling New Jersey’s worst cost-drivers: energy and school funding. Families are opening obscene utility bills averaging $800 a month, the direct result of Trenton’s reckless, unaffordable energy mandates that sidelined reliable nuclear energy and clean natural gas in favor of costly experiments. At the same time, a broken school funding formula has crushed rural and suburban towns, spiking property taxes while schools fire staff and cut programs. Energy and education are not luxuries — they are essentials. I will continue to fight to end Trenton’s tone-deaf policies, secure a fair school funding formula, and stabilize utility costs so families can afford to stay in New Jersey.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: The first step is electing Jack Ciattarelli as Governor. NJ cannot afford more progressive control that funds non-essentials. Affordability starts with fixing the flawed school funding formula, which has punished rural and suburban districts, driving up property taxes and forcing staff cuts. We must also reform energy policy, ending the governor’s costly mandates, restoring balance with reliable nuclear and natural gas, and lowering crushing utility bills, now $800 a month for many families. I’ve advanced legislation to grow apprenticeships so residents can train for good-paying jobs here at home. Republicans will reallocate wasteful spending on pork projects into essentials like schools, energy infrastructure, and direct taxpayer relief.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: New Jersey’s “affordable housing” law is crushing us. The Mount Laurel doctrine has morphed into a weapon of overreach, stripping local control and handing power to developers. In Cranbury, a 175-year family farm is being taken by eminent domain to meet bogus quotas. That’s appalling. Families lose land, while towns face sudden growth that roads, water, sewers, police, fire, and EMS cannot handle. Schools are already cutting staff, yet Trenton forces more density without classrooms to support it. Murphy and Democrats doubled down, ignoring warnings while siding with developers over families. Republicans will restore local control, protect farmland, ensure responsible growth, and fix the school funding formula so families can afford to stay.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: When we talk about “federal cuts,” much of this funding was never permanent — it was one-time COVID money. Building long-term programs on short-term dollars was irresponsible.

answers.Personal or professional background: Sales and Marketing executive with 35 years building experience in product development, market development and management. This experience has prepared me to understand how to understand problems and solve them in an organized and structured manner. We were a process manufacturer. When we had product complaints from customers it almost always meant that we had a process problem at the time the product was made. The last five years of my career were as an in-house consultant working on business process improvement projects.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: Our government in New Jersey has lost the confidence of many citizens. We have a process problem. When public policy more closely aligns with public opinion and the state does not seem to be run for the benefit of special interests, people will be more satisfied with government. This can only happen when we change the way we elect our government. The top issue for me is Electoral Reform followed by Government Reform. We must make the government more accountable to the people.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: We must take an analytical approach to identify the root causes for high property taxes and address those causes. We have over 530 municipalities in our state generating a lot of redundancy in local governments. We can do this without compromising the effectiveness of our government services or our schools. Services can be consolidated to achieve cost reductions. In our schools, Administration and overhead can be consolidated while student to teacher ratios and other elements of education delivery can be preserved.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: We have talked a good game on affordable housing but we’re not solving the problem. We need stronger funding for the affordable housing trust fund. Red tape and administrative delays for affordable housing projects must be reduced. And when an affordable housing project will impose unreasonable burdens on infrastructure including schools, the state should provide some assistance to minimize the impact on the local community.
answers.How would you manage federal funding cut: We are fortunate to have a surplus in our state finances. But we cannot be certain that we can replace all federal dollars that may be lost. We must set priorities and fund on the basis of those priorities. So identifying and prioritizing the more urgent needs will enable us to use our limited funds to maximum advantage.

answers.Personal or professional background: I bring over three decades of public service and policy experience to the New Jersey Legislature. Before my election to the Assembly, I served as District Director for U.S. Representative Rodney Frelinghuysen. I held roles on Capitol Hill as a Budget Analyst for the U.S. Senate Appropriations Committee and Policy Advisor for the House Veterans Affairs Committee. I also represented America’s Public Television Stations, Sesame Street, and Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood in Washington DC. One of my proudest accomplishments was working on the Clery Act to improve campus safety. I now focus on bipartisan solutions for children, families, and fiscal responsibility.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: Affordability. Our state budget has nearly doubled since the previous administration, and residents are bearing the cost through inflation and increased taxes on income, property, businesses, and more. I will continue to be a voice for fiscal responsibility and sound policy to prevent these costs from rising further. This means not only addressing the higher taxes residents face year after year but also tackling steep energy price hikes like we have seen across the state. My focus is on working across party lines to rein in spending, increase transparency, protect taxpayers, and keep New Jersey an affordable place to live, work, and raise a family.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: My approach includes delivering direct tax relief, such as expanding the child tax credit, increasing pension and retirement income exclusions, exempting essential items from sales tax, and restoring more Energy Tax Receipts funding to towns to ease property taxes. I also propose reforming the budget process by eliminating wasteful earmarks, requiring public disclosure of all spending items before a vote, and using independent revenue analysis to ensure accurate projections. These steps will help lower taxes, control spending, and make New Jersey a place where families can afford to live, work, and retire.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: No. While there is no disputing the critical need for affordable housing, I do not support a state- mandated, one-size-fits-all approach. This legislation places significant liability and economic burdens on taxpayers and undermines New Jersey’s long-standing principle of home rule, which ensures municipalities have the right to govern their own land-use planning.
answers.How would you manage federal funding cut: I have prioritized keeping essential programs like Medicaid, food assistance, and education that is strong and sustainable through legislation that promotes accountability and fiscal transparency. That includes enhancing oversight of public spending and adjusting reimbursement rates for critical Medicaid services. While I do not control federal funding decisions, I am committed to ensuring New Jersey continues to protect those most in need. As we navigate uncertain federal support, I will keep fighting for policies that use state resources efficiently and help families thrive.

answers.Personal or professional background: I am a civil engineer, Morristown Councilman, and candidate for the State Assembly. I grew up in a working-class union household and learned early the value of community and persistence. My wife and I are raising two daughters here, and I have built a career solving complex infrastructure challenges. I bring the same systems thinking to public service by fixing problems at their root, listening to the people affected, and delivering durable solutions. I believe the most important infrastructure is the kind we build around people.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: Rebuilding trust in government by delivering results people can see in their daily lives. That means investing in infrastructure, protecting public education, and making our communities affordable for working families. Too often leaders respond after a crisis. I believe in governing upstream and preventing problems before they land on a family’s doorstep.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: Reform school funding to stabilize local taxes, expand affordable housing options, and invest in infrastructure that lowers long-term costs. We can reduce property tax pressure by raising surplus caps for schools, modernizing special education reimbursement, and ensuring PILOT revenues support classrooms. I will also fight to rein in utility costs and protect residents from hidden fees.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: Yes. I support the new affordable housing law and will work to ensure towns meet their obligations. Housing costs are crushing families and we need a mix of strategies, including adaptive reuse of vacant properties, transit-oriented development, and stronger tenant protections. Affordable housing is key to attracting and retaining the workforce our communities depend on.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: We must protect vital services from federal shortfalls by building strong state-level backstops. That includes creating targeted reserve funds, improving efficiency in program delivery, and closing corporate tax loopholes that shift the burden onto working families. Every New Jerseyan should have access to healthcare, food, and quality education regardless of what happens in Washington.

answers.Occupation: Doctor of Clinical Nutrition/Small Business Owner
answers.Personal or professional background: Marisa is a Doctor of Clinical Nutrition, Registered Dietitian Nutritionist, Certified Specialist in Sports Dietetics, and Experienced Yoga Teacher. She is the Founder of Be Well Integrative Health Services, established in 2012, which is a wellness center headquartered in downtown Morristown, NJ. Be Well provides and is integrated into the medical teams of world-renowned medical practices nationwide. Marisa is also the Founder of The New Jersey VegFest: The Garden State’s Official Vegan Food Festival. answers.What is your top issue this year?: My top priorities are addressing and reducing the high cost of living: utilites bills, housing, healthare, etc. Also, I am prioritizing supporting small businesses and economic growth, and promoting government transparency and accountability. These issues impact every resident, and I am committed to practical, equitable solutions that improve daily life, strengthen communities, and ensure New Jersey remains a great place to live and work.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: To make New Jersey more affordable, I will work to lower utility bills by supporting local renewable energy, modernizing the grid, and reforming market structures that drive up costs. I will advocate for the preservation of social programs that have been proven to be fiscally responsible, expand access to affordable housing, and support policies that reduce everyday expenses such as healthcare, childcare, and transportation. I am committed to ensuring state government spends efficiently, prioritizing programs that directly benefit residents while protecting quality of life and essential services.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: I support law designed to increase affordable housing because every New Jersey resident deserves access to safe, stable, and reasonably priced housing. I also believe we must continue to expand housing options through incentives for responsible development, preservation of existing affordable housing, and streamlining permitting processes to reduce unnecessary costs. Additionally, I will advocate for programs that help first-time homebuyers and middle-income families, ensuring that housing is accessible and sustainable without overburdening taxpayers or compromising community resources.
answers.How would you manage federal funding cut: The state should respond to federal funding cuts by protecting vulnerable residents and ensuring essential services remain strong. This includes prioritizing state budgets to maintain Medicaid, food assistance, and education programs, finding efficiencies without reducing quality, and seeking alternative funding sources such as public-private partnerships and targeted grants. New Jersey must also advocate at the federal level for equitable funding and policies that support our communities, ensuring that families, students, and seniors do not bear the brunt of reduced federal support.

answers.Personal or professional background: A lifelong educator and public servant, I serve as Principal/Superintendent and Assemblywoman for New Jersey’s 27th Legislative District. As the daughter of immigrants and a mother of three, I bring both lived experience and professional expertise to my work, championing education equity, reproductive freedom, and government transparency to create a more just and inclusive New Jersey.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: Affordability is my top issue this election. Families are struggling with the rising housing costs, healthcare, and everyday expenses. I am focused on making New Jersey more affordable for families and seniors, working to expand access to quality, affordable childcare, strengthen property tax relief through programs like ANCHOR and Senior Freeze, and create pathways to homeownership. I also support Retire Ready, a program that helps small business employees save for retirement when traditional plans like 401Ks are not available, bridging the gap for workers and promoting long-term financial security.

I’m advancing legislation to expand access to affordable childcare, free school meals, and create affordable homeownership pathways, especially for first-time buyers. I continue to support programs like ANCHOR, Senior Freeze, and StayNJ to deliver meaningful property tax relief and help seniors age in place with financial security.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: Yes, I support the law to increase affordable housing. New Jersey must do more to ensure that seniors, veterans, working families, and disabled communities can afford to live here. I also support streamlining local zoning and incentivizing mixed-income development to boost housing supply while preserving community character. At the same time, we must consider each community’s infrastructure and school capacity to ensure responsible growth with purpose, while preserving green spaces and promoting environmentally sound building practices and green initiatives.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: We must protect our most critical services. I will advocate for the strategic use of state surplus funds, prioritize programs that serve vulnerable populations, and ensure every dollar is spent effectively.

answers.Personal or professional background: I am married, the father of triplets and an observant Jew. I lived in New Jersey my entire life. I grew up in Maplewood and graduated Columbia High School, I graduated Colgate University and earned two masters degrees at Teachers College Columbia University. answers.What is your top issue this year?: Make New Jersey affordable and return to the principles of the state moto Liberty and Prosperity. We need to limit the size and scope of government, limit the power of public employee unions. We need us free market principles of land use and have property rights to expand the housing supply so people can afford to live here.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: Make us less litigious by having those who bring legal action and loose will have to pay the legal cost of the other side. Reduce of eliminate zoning rules so housing supply can expand based on free markets and reduce prices. Limit the power of public employee unions. We need to move our employees into a 401 K type pension and health care saving accounts for health care in retirement. I would require all school districts to merge in to a per K to 12 system and eliminate sending a receiving districts. I would demand reduction in administrative cost from hospitals or they would be subject to reduced state aid.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: No – Housing and rent should be market based. We push back on zoning rules and radically expand the housing supply to reduce housing costs
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: Require health care providers to be more efficient and cut cost on administration. Allow non doctors to do more of the simple stuff in medical care and keep the complex stuff for the physicians.

answers.Personal or professional background: My career began at NJ Network, where I worked on Images/Imagenes, a program highlighting cultural events and public affairs in Latino communities. answers.What is your top issue this year?: Throughout my first year in the Legislature, my top priorities have been addressing climate change and protecting immigrant communities. Regardless of the outcome, I remain committed to fighting for our environment and safeguarding our communities, and I plan to continue building broad coalitions next session to ensure these critical protections are enacted and sustained.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: Making New Jersey more affordable requires both immediate relief and long-term solutions. I support expanding property tax relief programs like ANCHOR and Senior Freeze to ease burdens on homeowners and renters. We must invest in affordable housing, strengthen tenant protections, and expand access to childcare, one of the largest costs families face. Streamlining professional licensing and lowering health insurance costs will help more people join the workforce and support small businesses. Finally, ensuring fair wages will help working families make ends meet. Affordability must remain central to every policy decision so residents can thrive in our state.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: Yes, I do support the state law designed to increase the amount of affordable housing.
answers.How would you manage federal funding cut: I believe the state must actively advocate with our federal partners to restore and protect funding for these critical programs. At the same time, we need to strengthen state-level solutions to ensure that our communities are safeguarded, even in the face of cuts. This means improving coordination across state, county, and municipal governments so that resources are used as efficiently as possible. We should also identify areas where costs can be reduced without harming essential services, and ensure that communication across all levels of government is clear, direct, and effective.

answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: Housing is the largest monthly expense for most families, so we have to start there. This is about dollars and sense, and what we value as a state. No one should lose their job, health care, or housing over this.

answers.Do you support the state law designed to: Yes, I support the state law designed to increase the amount of affordable housing. We can also explore new partnerships, and invest in programs that save money in the long run. In tough times, it is critical that we don’t pass the burden onto New Jersey families.

answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: I am the prime sponsor of A-1920, which extends childcare subsidies to families earning up to 300 percent of federal poverty level. answers.What is your top issue this year?: Democracy. Democracy. Democracy. We are living in strange times and everyone must work together to preserve our way of life. We are in danger of losing our Democracy as we barrel head-long in being an Oligarchy. Everyone I speak to is frightened. Everyone’s way of life is threatened.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: To me the most obvious involves what is one of the things most dear to New Jerseyans–that is home rule. We have 565 municipalities in NJ and each of us are proud of and cling to our hometowns. But we have to start to consolidate services. We no longer have the luxury of 565 Super. of Schools or 565 Police Chiefs. Some smaller towns have to start taking a hard look at shared services: DPW, Recycling, local courts, etc.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: All lives have always been centered around the home, be it a campfire, a one-bedroom apartment or a mansion. Without stable, affordable housing our everyday lives are uncertain and it is impossible to perform to our potential–it is also inhumane. I am a strong proponent of affordable housing;
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: As a member of BNBMC foundation board, and the Chairperson of Bergen County Community Development I see these, and other organizations I am or have been (BOE) a part of, scrambling to find ways to make up the shortfalls. It is not a question that can be answered in 100 words, or 10,000 words. Managing these cuts will take a concerted effort of professionals, elected officials, community members and volunteers. Although the task might seems monumental, I trust in collaborative work and believe we will find ways to serve the needy among us and keep our schools strong.

answers.Personal or professional background: Former Dumont Mayor Andrew LaBruno (LD39) has spent the past decade revitalizing his community and championing public safety. answers.What is your top issue this year?: Affordability is the top issue for New Jersey families, seniors, and young professionals alike. Property taxes remain among the highest in the nation, and rising costs for housing, healthcare, and everyday necessities are pushing residents to the brink—or out of the state entirely.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: Solutions to make NJ more affordable should focus on but not limited to:
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: New Jersey’s current affordable housing structure is both unsustainable for many suburban municipalities. Most small towns lack the open, developable land and infrastructure needed to support large-scale housing developments. Yet the state continues to impose unfunded mandates that place undue strain on these communities. While affordable housing is vital, legislators must rethink the system—shifting the burden away from towns that simply cannot absorb it, incentivizing development and funding infrastructure where it’s feasible, and restructuring how housing is allocated. When small municipalities build affordable units, priority access should be given to residents from their community and surrounding region to preserve local stability.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: Managing potential federal funding cuts requires a proactive, strategic approach focused on protecting essential services while maximizing efficiency. First, the state must conduct a thorough audit of existing programs to eliminate waste and redirect funds to high-priority areas like healthcare, education, and social services. We must also strengthen public-private partnerships and pursue alternative funding sources, including grants and innovation-driven initiatives. Additionally, working collaboratively with local governments to expand shared services and consolidate where appropriate can stretch limited resources.

answers.Occupation: Chief Executive Officer, Ranch Hope Inc.
answers.Personal or professional background: It’s an honor to serve as State Assemblyman for New Jersey’s Third Legislative District, building on my lifelong commitment to serving children, youth, and families. As CEO of Ranch Hope, a faith-based nonprofit, I lead 200 dedicated staff supporting vulnerable youth across South Jersey. With over 30 years of experience, I’ve worked across government and community sectors to advocate for policies that make a difference. I hold a master’s in nonprofit management from Eastern University, volunteer with Meals on Wheels, and am a proud member of the Rotary Club of Woodstown. My wife Julie and I live in Woodstown and have three adult children.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: Our state is facing an affordability crisis that’s hitting families especially hard. From rising property taxes and utility bills to healthcare, childcare, and groceries, the cost of living is stretching household budgets thin. We must hold the line on taxes, deliver the promised 50% property tax cut for seniors, and expand relief for working families. I support limiting utility rate hikes, increasing energy production, and investing in rural communities through agriculture, transportation, and small business support. My focus is on fighting for South Jersey to get its fair share—and for government to make life more affordable for everyone.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: South Jersey is in the grip of an affordability crisis that’s straining household budgets and holding back our economy. From rising property taxes to utility bills, groceries, and healthcare, working families are being squeezed. Tackling this requires real action—capping utility rate hikes, delivering tax relief for seniors, and investing in rural communities. That means supporting family farms, expanding high-speed internet, and growing local businesses. A stronger, more affordable South Jersey starts with a fair economy that works for everyone—not just a few. We must ensure our region gets its fair share and the tools needed to thrive.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: Affordable housing is a vital part of addressing New Jersey’s affordability crisis, especially for young people looking to build their future here. We must support first-time homebuyers, veterans, and working families without compromising the character, history, or tourism that define our communities. Thoughtful, well-planned development can expand housing options while preserving what makes our towns unique. By doing so, we strengthen local economies, support schools and small businesses, and give more families the opportunity to put down roots and thrive.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: New Jersey’s rising state budget and looming federal cuts to healthcare and education put our most vulnerable communities at risk—especially in rural South Jersey, where healthcare deserts already exist. I support a fiscally responsible approach that lowers taxes, reins in spending, and ensures every dollar is used wisely. With one of the lowest returns on the tax dollars we send to Washington, we must fight back against unfair federal cuts that threaten hospitals, clinics, and patient care. By focusing on smart, efficient spending, we can protect essential services, support rural communities, and make life more affordable for all New Jerseyans.

answers.Occupation: Vice President, Workforce Innovation and Partnerships – Rowan College of South Jersey
answers.Personal or professional background: I’m running for reelection because South Jersey families deserve real solutions—not soundbites—on rising costs, healthcare, and opportunity for the next generation. I proudly represent the 3rd Legislative District, fighting to cap utility rate hikes and expand access to menopause-related care. As a Gloucester County Commissioner, I launched a $15 million small business loan fund that created over 400 jobs. With 30 years in public education, I now serve as Vice President at Rowan College of South Jersey. As a kidney transplant recipient, I know firsthand how a catastrophic illness can turn your life upside down—and why access to quality, affordable healthcare isn’t a luxury, it’s a necessity.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: Affordability is the most pressing issue facing our families, from rising utility bills to grocery cost and property taxes. I’ve felt those struggles too, which is why I authored the Electric Bill Cap Act to limit rate hikes and sponsored grants to help small businesses recover from construction impacts. I also passed a bipartisan law targeting organized retail theft. In a divided climate, I’ve proven we can still work together. I’m committed to practical solutions—expanding workforce training, improving education and healthcare access, and ensuring South Jersey gets its fair share—so families aren’t punished just for getting sick.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: Rising costs—from utilities to groceries—are straining New Jersey families. I introduced the Electric Bill Cap Act to limit utility rate hikes for households earning up to $120,000 and sponsored grants to help small businesses impacted by public construction. I also passed a bipartisan law targeting organized retail theft that drives up prices. I’m committed to practical, fiscally responsible solutions: expanding workforce training, improving healthcare access, and ensuring South Jersey gets its fair share. My priority is making our communities more affordable and supporting working families with policies that deliver real, lasting relief.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: Affordable housing is a critical part of addressing New Jersey’s affordability crisis. We must support first-time homebuyers, veterans, and working families so they can live in safe, welcoming communities of their choice. That means expanding housing options through strong partnerships with municipalities and by leveraging state and federal resources to meet local needs. Expanding housing options in a way that aligns with local planning strengthens our economy, supports schools and small businesses, and helps families put down roots.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: I believe in a fiscally responsible approach to government that lowers taxes, reduces wasteful spending, and protects New Jersey taxpayers. Our state already receives one of the lowest returns on the dollars we send to Washington, and I’m standing up to harmful federal cuts that threaten essential services. By prioritizing smart budgeting and efficient use of resources, we can ease the burden on working families while investing in the services our communities rely on. New Jersey taxpayers deserve fairness and accountability—both in Trenton and in Washington.

answers.Personal or professional background: Chris Konawel is a lifelong South Jersey resident, raised in South Harrison Township and now living in Glassboro. With a background in sales and finance from his family’s small business, he brings real-world experience and what he proudly calls a PhD in life experience. Now in his fourth year as a Gloucester County Commissioner, Chris is known for his no-nonsense, solutions-focused leadership, championing fiscal responsibility and transparency. A longtime martial artist with over 15 years of Brazilian Jiu Jitsu training, he applies grit and discipline to every challenge.
answers.What is your top issue this year?: I am committed to addressing the fiscal crisis facing our community by cutting wasteful spending and ensuring tax relief for working families. I will focus on transparency and accountability, and make sure residents know how their tax dollars are used. I will immediately work to resolve school funding disparities that disproportionately affect south Jersey and tackle the insane utility bills that are putting financial strain on families. I am an advocate for small business, i support policies that foster economic growth and job creation. I will always stand with law enforcement to keep communities safe, and lead with ethical, principled decisions.
answers.What are your specific proposals for mak: New Jersey’s fiscal health has been strained for years, burdened by excessive debt, unsustainable spending, and an over-reliance on temporary financial fixes. The state’s budget is too often marked by inefficiencies, high borrowing, and rising taxes, creating an environment where middle-class families and businesses bear the brunt. To achieve long-term economic stability and make New Jersey more affordable for residents, a comprehensive fiscal responsibility and budget reform plan is essential.
answers.Do you support the state law designed to: New Jersey residents are burdened by some of the highest housing costs in the nation, including expensive rents and skyrocketing property taxes. While increasing the stock of low-income housing is a solution some advocate for, I believe there are other ways to reduce housing costs without mandating additional low-income housing. Through zoning reforms, incentivizing affordable housing development, reducing property taxes, and supporting first-time homebuyers, we can significantly lower housing costs for all New Jersey residents.
answers.How would you manage potential federal f: Managing healthcare/social services/education cuts due to reductions in federal support is an immense challenge for any state. New Jersey, in particular, faces significant pressure to continue providing essential services despite these challenges. The key to successfully managing funding cuts lies in a combination of strategic use of state resources, promoting efficiency, and pursuing innovative solutions.

answers.Personal background: Before serving in elected office, I worked as an investigative journalist at KYW-TV for 17 years. I won 38 Emmy Awards for my reporting protecting consumer rights and investigating unscrupulous or unethical businesses. I have been a member of the American Federation of Television and Radio Artists (AFTRA) for 38 years, and have served six years as an AFTRA shop steward. I have a bachelor’s degree in communications from Temple University and live in Washington Township with my wife, Lisa, my daughter, Meghan, and our dog, Chloe.
answers.Political background: I served as mayor of Washington Township from 2005 to 2009 and have represented the 4th Legislative District since 2006. In the General Assembly, I serve as the deputy speaker and chairman of the Assembly’s Consumer Affairs Committee, where I fight for open government, increased education funding, property tax relief and the elimination of waste and inefficiency. Throughout my career in the Assembly, I have sponsored legislation to make government more responsive and accountable, reform commissions and independent authorities, and require government workers to live in New Jersey. I have also sponsored numerous bills to increase consumer awareness and protection, including measures to improve product safety and the safety of children’s toys.
answers.Why are you running for office?: I’m running for the same reasons that motivated me to first run for office years ago: because I love our state and I want us to continue to grow and prosper, and to do that we need to cut down on crushing taxes and waste.
answers.Key election issue: New Jersey’s unaffordably high property taxes.
answers.Example of a successful project: Local tax rates used to rise uncontrollably, sometimes as much as 7% in a year, and I sponsored a law that prohibited municipalities and school districts from raising taxes more than 2% in any given year. That change has saved New Jersey families thousands of dollars, and I’m proud to have helped make this state more affordable.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: Working as an investigative reporter, I often had to deal with dishonest businesses and scammers trying to pull the wool over my eyes. Through those experiences and challenges, I’ve learned to always ask questions and stand up for people who are being taken advantage of.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: I support our firearms laws that ensure that we keep guns out of the hands of people who should not have them, while still respecting our constitutional rights. I’m proud to have earned the endorsement of Brady and support of Moms Demand Action, the two leading gun safety groups in America.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: I support the goal of tackling climate change by building new green energy sources, but I do not support mandates for individuals. We need to help people make changes, not force them.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: Along with sponsoring StayNJ, I sponsored legislation to expand the Senior Freeze and voted twice to support the ANCHOR tax rebates. I plan to keep fighting in the Senate to bring property taxes, housing costs and rents down.

answers.Personal background: During my 27-year career as a bankruptcy attorney, I have helped over 7,500 people save their homes and cars and obtain relief from crushing debt. I also serve as the Gloucester County regional coordinator for the Financial Literacy Program, visiting high schools throughout Camden and Gloucester counties to discuss the pitfalls of obtaining and using credit unwisely. I have lived with my wife, Karen, in Gloucester Township since 1995, where we raised our four children, Katie, Shawn, Nick and Brian. I earned my J.D. from Widener University Law School and am currently working on obtaining a master’s degree in law at St. John’s University. In my free time, I coach youth in soccer, baseball and basketball, and serve as a soccer commissioner and Tiger Scout den leader.
answers.Political background: In my five terms as a Gloucester Township councilman, I have been a staunch advocate for fiscal responsibility, lowering property taxes, economic development, investing in youth and community safety. In the General Assembly I plan to fight to make New Jersey a place where working people can afford a home and raise a family.
answers.Key election issue: New Jersey is increasingly unaffordable for working people.
answers.Example of a successful project: I’ve built my own law practice that has helped thousands of people navigate debt and bankruptcy and keep their homes and cars safe. I’m extremely proud of the work my firm has done protecting those in need, and I consider it an honor to have built a successful business.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: Food insecurity as a child. I grew up in a low-income household, and we had little in the fridge. In college I didn’t have enough money to live on campus, so friends of mine let me sleep on their floor and would sneak me into the dining hall since I couldn’t afford to eat there. A woman from Trenton came to the back of the dining hall after noticing my situation and displayed immense kindness by saying that I was welcome to eat for free. Growing up with so little was not an easy experience, but it taught me perseverance, patience and, above all, trust in the goodness of others.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: We need strong gun laws, and my campaign is proud to have support from national leaders in gun violence prevention like Brady and Moms Demand Action.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: Climate change is an existential threat and we need to take action, but we should not be enacting onerous requirements on regular families. I would move the clean energy transition forward through building renewables and providing incentives for upgrades, not through individual mandates.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: The StayNJ law will provide immense relief for many New Jersey homeowners, and along with that law, I support increasing our overall housing options through smart and sustainable development.

answers.Personal background: I’m the son of a single mom who raised the four of us by herself with the help of her family when we lost our home when I was 7. I’m currently enrolled in the Doctorate of Higher Education Leadership program at Rowan University and am a volunteer firefighter with Williamstown Fire Company #1. I work full time at Rowan College of South Jersey as the director of the foundation and alumni relations. I earned my associate’s degree at Gloucester County College (now Rowan College of South Jersey) before going to Rutgers Camden, where I earned my bachelor’s in history and political science and my master’s in public administration. While I was earning my degrees, I served on the board of trustees of Gloucester County College.
answers.Political background: I was the youngest Democratic council member elected in Monroe Township’s history at age 23, where I worked with the mayor to curb substance abuse and create the local Market-to-Affordable Housing Program. I also helped introduce four municipal budgets with a 0% tax increase. In 2021 I was elected to the board of education, where I helped secure over $25 million for capital energy improvements through the state Energy Savings Improvement Program, resulting in significant school upgrades at no cost to taxpayers. I also helped initiate full-day pre-K and fought for funding to increase the number of families with access. In 2022, serving as board of education president, I was the first BOE president to lower school taxes.
answers.Why are you running for office?: I’ve always had a passion for helping people because I went through struggles growing up as the son of a single mom, and I’m running because decisions are being made that impact young people across the state without young people being in the room. If elected I would be one of the few millennial legislators in the state, and that’s important in the face of the challenges that New Jersey is confronting.
answers.Key election issue: Affordability, plain and simple.
answers.Example of a successful project: Implementing full-day pre-K in Monroe public schools. We used to not have full-day pre-K, but with the board of education, I worked to provide the capacity to offer it to families across the township.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: Growing up I had to fend for myself and work to put myself through college, because my family didn’t have the financial resources. I helped as family members battled substance abuse and was the first in my family to go to college, while some family members didn’t even make it through high school. Thanks to my grandparents, my younger sister and I made it through school and got the education needed to succeed in life, and I want to help others have those same opportunities.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: We need to ensure that we keep guns out of the hands of criminals, but I support individuals’ right to bear arms.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: I support the goal of tackling climate change, but not the choice to make individual citizens bear the responsibility alone. Instead of mandates, we should provide incentives to help people do the right thing.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: StayNJ, municipal consolidation and expanding housing opportunities, especially for young families and first-time homebuyers.
