answers.Personal background: I was born in Brooklyn and was educated at Vassar College, Johns Hopkins University and the Georgetown University Law Center. Prior to becoming a legislator, I was a senior staff attorney at the Community Health Law Project and served as a deputy attorney general in the Division of Criminal Justice in Trenton and as an assistant district attorney in Philadelphia. I also served as a clinical associate professor at Seton Hall Law School.
answers.Political background: My career in public service started on the West Windsor-Plainsboro School Board in 1992. In 1995, I was elected to the Plainsboro Township Committee. In 2000, I was elected to represent LD14 as an assemblywoman and in 2010 I was elected to the State Senate. Now, I serve as chair of the Law and Public Safety Committee, vice cair of the Environment and Energy Committee and a member of the Budget and Appropriations Committee. I am also co-chair of the Legislative Manufacturing Caucus.
answers.Why are you running for office?: I’m running for office again this year because there is a lot of work that still needs to be done to keep New Jersey one of the best places in the nation to live, work and learn. I am a strong advocate for working families, education, the environment and our first responders – and I would continue that track record if re-elected.
answers.Key election issue: There are many. As your senator, I have and would continue to champion initiatives that protect the environment, ensure drinking water is free from contaminants (like PFAS), promote public health and safety, defend working families, and continue to make New Jersey a place where families can get best-in-the-nation education, good jobs, and good housing.
answers.Example of a successful project: In 2017, I had the opportunity to co-chair the Joint Legislative Task Force on Drinking Water Infrastructure. This task force was one of the first things we did to address water issues, and was the impetus for some of the things we’ve undertaken in following years. At the time, the task force took testimony from various stakeholders and concluded that lead service lines, combined sewer overflows and flooding threaten New Jersey residents’ health, safety and economic well being. Being co-chair of the task force allowed me to introduce bills and advocate for their passage to make New Jersey’s water infrastructure more reliable, safe, and sustainable. Through my co-chairmanship of this task force, I was able to, for example, sponsor and pass legislation providing for the removal of lead service lines. I’m able to continue the work to protect clean drinking water by now tackling emerging contaminants (like PFAS) and the spread of diseases like Legionnaire’s. I also sponsored a significant police licensing program last year for all New Jersey law enforcement officers. Again, it took a lot of effort to get everyone on the same page, but we did it.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: I pride myself on my consensus-building skills. When working to enact policy, I make it a priority to get stakeholders from all sides of an issue in a room together to hash out a middle ground. One bill I was recently able to do this with is S287. S287 was a bill I introduced to incentivize the use of low-carbon concrete – a new technology that will help reduce greenhouse gas emissions in our building sector. Upon the bill’s introduction, labor groups, business and manufacturing groups were all skeptical. As someone who prides myself on strong environmental, labor and manufacturing track records, I took each of their concerns seriously and tried to help them work out their differences. I spent months going back and forth with each group, proposing different iterations of the bill, until we were able to get all stakeholders – and the governor–- on board. I was incredibly pleased to see S287 signed into law last year.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: New Jersey already has strict gun laws. I believe we really are a leader in this regard, already ahead of many other states – for example, we passed seven new gun safety laws just last July. That said, I have always been a proponent of strong gun laws, and as chair of the Senate Law and Public Safety Committee, I’ve had the chance to work on a lot of these issues. I was the co-prime sponsor of the recent “conceal carry” law (S3214) passed in response to Bruen. S3214 is now in the court’s hands, and until we have a decision, we don’t know what follow-up legislation is needed. Otherwise, I was the prime sponsor of a bill just signed by the governor (S3150) that establishes strict penalties for firearm trafficking that results in injury or death. I also sponsored a law (2018’s S2374) that required background checks for private gun sales. Through my committee, we’ve also discussed safe storage, gun violence prevention programs, updates to training and application requirements and more.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: Generally, I support our state’s shift to greener, renewable technologies. I was a prime sponsor of the bill (S2252) that established New Jersey’s electric vehicle rebate program, along with many others to expand the use of solar technology. The reason our solar and electric vehicle programs have been so successful is that they provide financial incentives to try out new technologies. I’m not convinced that we are ready to mandate the decarbonization of public and private buildings by switching from natural gas to electric heat and cooking. It’s important that we not mandate changes without fully understanding how this will affect families and the economy. Anything we do related to clean energy would also have to take into account and prioritize New Jersey’s own skilled labor workforce and local jobs.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: New Jersey lacks an adequate affordable housing stock, and we need to do more to make New Jersey affordable. This year, I sponsored a budget resolution to return $150 million in Energy Tax Receipts to the municipalities. This money will be used locally to help provide property tax relief. We also passed a few bills this session helping first-time buyers afford to purchase homes, as another example. We have also made major investments in new and/or expanded property tax relief programs. Just in the last year, New Jersey homeowners and renters received their first ever ANCHOR check in the mail. This year, the Legislature expanded those benefits. We passed STAY NJ into law, to reduce the property tax burden on our seniors. And we expanded the Senior Freeze program so that more individuals qualify. Outside of these programs, we must continue to work toward fully funding our schools, keeping property taxes in check, and expanding assistance programs for those who need it.

answers.Personal background: I am a native of Mercer County residing in Trenton. After graduating high school, I worked as a secretary to put myself through Mercer County Community College and nursing school. I worked as a critical care nurse at Fox Chase Cancer Institute for five years before opening my own child care business. I am presently the Mercer County representative for the AFSCME NJ, which represents early childhood education workers, attorneys and judiciary employees, behavioral health, corrections, emergency services, health care, law enforcement, etc. I invented a medical feeding device called Nutra2Go for my husband who was diagnosed with esophageal cancer in 2000. This spurred the creation of Mobile Solutions International, a medical startup that champions my invention. I served as vice president of the company for three years. During the pandemic, I formed a volunteer team of 30 to produce 7,000 face masks for the Trenton Police and Fire Departments, State Police and others.
answers.Political background: I was inspired to enter the political arena because of my experiences during the pandemic. I learned how to advocate for my patients when I was a nurse and I wanted to advocate for the people of New Jersey affected by the pandemic and the policies in Trenton. I first ran for General Assembly in the 15th Legislative District in 2021. I learned quickly from my time campaigning and I was honored when I was asked to run for the Senate in the 14th Legislative District this year. I plan on fighting for the residents of the 14th District the way I fight for my patients and their families.
answers.Why are you running for office?: I am running for office because the quality of life is going down and the cost of living is going up in New Jersey. This is forcing many residents who have lived here their entire lives to leave the state to be able to retire. Our high tax rate is preventing businesses from investing here and many small businesses are closing shop. The people of our state are losing faith in their government that the State of New Jersey will become affordable for the average family again. As a nurse I learned to advocate for my patients. I want to use those same skills to advocate for the people in my legislative district. We can fix New Jersey and make it the great place to live, work and retire that it once was.
answers.Key election issue: Parental rights
answers.Example of a successful project: During the pandemic I formed a group of 30 volunteers to make face masks for three area hospitals, four fire companies, the Trenton Police, the State Police, commercial drivers, office workers and other essential personnel who could not work without face masks. I made this contribution because I could not return to my role as a nurse because I am the primary caregiver for my mother and husband, who could not be exposed to COVID because of prior health conditions. I organized my group remotely, starting by designing the pattern, collecting donated fabrics and organizing sewers, cutters and drivers to deliver the masks. As a result of our efforts, we donated more than 7,000 masks to those in need. On behalf of the group, I was awarded the Hero’s Award from AFSCME NJ Union for 2021 for the work that was done.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: As a nurse working in the field of cancer, I found that you were continually being challenged, nothing was the same, every day brought new challenges, one patient was not the same as another. Our floor was critical care, we worked as a team, a nurse and a doctor for each shift. I had to be creative, I had to understand the needs of not just the patient but the family as well. Every day you had to dig down deep to find the positivity in the job so the death of a patient you learned to love did not stop you from giving to the new patient that came onto the floor hours after the death of another. Dealing with critical care cancer patients is much different and more difficult than other areas of nursing, only 1 in 10 make it.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: First and foremost, I stand with the citizens of New Jersey who own and use firearms responsibly. Punishing law-abiding citizens for the actions of criminals will not stop gun violence or solve issues with crime in New Jersey’s cities. If we want to reduce gun violence, we must start by enforcing the laws already on the books. We must support police in their efforts to make our communities safer and prosecutors must enforce laws in our cities instead of allowing violent offenders to be released. Gun violence is only one of many crimes that is on the rise in New Jersey due to Trenton and Washington Democrats being lenient on criminals.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: The only green thing about Gov. Phil Murphy’s energy plan is the money being pocketed by the environmental lobbyists. The worst environmental project being pushed by Democrats in New Jersey are some 3,400 wind turbines being built off the shore. These are known to be responsible for the death of whales, dolphins and other marine animals, and they will negatively impact commercial and recreational fishing, military operations, navigational safety and more. The wind turbines will also be visible from the shore, each the size of the Chrysler Building in New York City, and will devastate the tourist industry in our shore towns. Residents of New Jersey want a responsible energy plan that will deal with climate change, reduce costs and provide reliability. The plan being put forward by Trenton Democrats does not accomplish these goals and only punishes responsible residents with increased costs and outrageous restrictions like no plastic bags at stores or no gas stoves at home.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: The cost of living in New Jersey has increased every year under Gov. Phil Murphy and Trenton Democrats. To address the increase in costs to gas, food, household goods and the housing market we must elect responsible leaders who will reduce taxes, remove burdensome regulations and cut government red tape. As a senator I will put forward policies and vote for legislation to reduce taxes, provide fair school funding, reduce useless regulations and make it easier for businesses to operate in New Jersey.

answers.Personal background: I was born in Egypt and migrated to New Jersey with my family when I was 3 years old. I grew up in North Edison and attended Edison public schools from kindergarten through high school graduation. I received my bachelor’s degree from Rutgers University in 2010 and graduated from Rutgers Law School of Camden with honors in 2013. I started my legal career as an assistant prosecutor in the Burlington County Prosecutor’s Office and in 2018 co-founded the law firm of Elias & Gonzalez LLC in Perth Amboy. I am married with three children, 5 years old and younger. I am also a mortgage loan originator and own two coffee shops with my wife in Jamesburg and Hamilton and own multiple rental properties in Central Jersey.
answers.Political background: I began my political career in 2021 when I ran for State Senate in the 14th Legislative District. This is my second race for a seat in the State Legislature.
answers.Why are you running for office?: I am running for office to bring the next generation of leadership to New Jersey. I have lived in New Jersey my entire life and am invested both personally and professionally in the success of our state’s future. I want to bring a fresh perspective to Trenton as a parent, an attorney and small business owner that lives through and understands the challenges facing families and businesses in New Jersey in the 21st century.
answers.Key election issue: A key issue for me is the affordability crisis that makes New Jersey one of the hardest states in the country to raise a family, start a business or retire.
answers.Example of a successful project: Serving as a managing partner of a law firm that was founded five years ago with two lawyers, two paralegals and one office, that has since grown to a law firm with two offices and a highly diverse staff consisting of four lawyers, six paralegals and a 500% increase in gross revenue in just five years.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: It has been challenging for me to run a campaign for state office while raising three young children with my wife and operating multiple businesses at the same time. I have overcome those challenges by taking life one day at a time and surrounding myself with supportive, loving and encouraging people that keep me motivated and on the path of success.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: Our Founding Fathers believed the right to bear arms was so important that they specifically enumerated in our Bill of Rights that “the right of people to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed.” While I believe that there are some exceptions for people who should not be allowed to own firearms for the safety of themselves and others, I do not think our state lawmakers need to take any measures at this time beyond what has already been deemed reasonably necessary by existing state and federal law to balance the need for public safety with the binding authority of the U.S. Constitution.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: I would call on the Murphy administration to collaborate with the Legislature on setting these policies rather than establishing them by executive order. Major policies that have a lasting impact on New Jersey residents should be brought before those elected to represent their interests, only after those representatives have had a reasonable and meaningful opportunity to hear testimony from industry experts on environmental challenges specific to New Jersey and the most responsible (and affordable) ways to address them.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: The most immediate and effective way to address the cost of rent, housing affordability and ever-increasing property taxes in New Jersey is to tie the school funding to the state income tax as intended when the income tax was introduced in 1976. This will allow higher income earners who are more likely to have children in school to bear the cost of their education, while allowing seniors and lower-income households who are in lower tax brackets to afford their mortgages or their rent on homes that currently pay up to 60 cents on the property tax dollar to the local school district.

answers.Personal background: What is my foundation?
answers.Political background: I recently served under my sixth governor as the assistant commissioner of human capital strategies and project management lead for public apprenticeships to the New Jersey Department of Labor and Workforce Development. I was honored to contribute to the Murphy-Oliver administration and continue my great-grandfather Samuel McCoy’s legacy, who proudly served Gov. Woodrow Wilson as the State House elevator operator. I’ve been an elected committee person in Hamilton for over a decade.
answers.Why are you running for office?: Due to my deep commitment to my community. What are my community service efforts?
answers.Key election issue: My pursuit of your support is based on my firm belief that my education, professional experiences and community involvement will contribute greatly to representing the needs of our constituents. Investing more in public safety, addressing the pressing issues facing our community, such as economic development and closing talent gaps while working to keep our tax burden low, are at the forefront of my agenda. Suppose I am fortunate enough to win this election, you will have my commitment to work tirelessly to bring more resources and investments into our district and to collaborate with partners across the state to identify strategies to ensure a sustainable future. I believe that by forming strong partnerships with stakeholders across sectors, we can achieve greater impact and create lasting change. I value your input and advice on the district’s strategic plan and ask for your support.
answers.Example of a successful project: Helped position the city of Philadelphia and the Wells Fargo Center as the DNC 2016 convention site ($10 million budget). Leveraged connections at the DNC to prepare the mayor and Wells Fargo, including transportation, safety, dining and entertainment – as sports and entertainment HR manager.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: As we witness dynamic shifts in the economy, we must make sure we are supporting economic growth by bringing in companies that can thrive with our workforce. We have a very educated population and have brilliant tradesmen to fill the gaps. It is paramount that we adapt and evolve to foster growth and prosperity mutually for businesses and our residents.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: New Jersey has some of the best gun laws in the nation. I will continue to advocate for gun violence prevention and will govern with gun safety in mind.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: Making further investments in electric vehicle (EV) infrastructure to reduce reliance on diesel fuels. As of late, there are not enough EV charging stations for fleets of EVs.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: There is an increased number of large corporations, LLCs, and private organizations buying up our homes and pricing out the middle class. We should introduce legislation that can help first-time homeowners purchase homes affordably. As a licensed New Jersey Realtor, I believe increasing the number of affordable housing developments and supporting organizations, like Homefront, that rehab homes and making them available to families for purchase will increase inventory. I will continue to analyze the state’s revenue to introduce new tax abatement programs. Lastly, I’m looking to draft legislation making it mandatory for lenders to accept partial payments.

answers.Personal background: Born in Point Pleasant but was blessed to grow up in rural Montana, the ultimate free-range childhood. My last two years of high school was home school, a conservative faith-based curriculum that instilled in me a strong love of country, the Constitution and a desire to do public service. Intellectually, it also prepared me well for college, where I started pre-nursing. A sense of adventure moved me to Kentucky, South Carolina, back to Montana and finally to New Jersey in 2003 where I finished my education as a cardiovascular technologist. While I always worked in health care full time, I had side jobs as a horse trainer and in fitness.
answers.Political background: At 18 I registered as a Republican and began a career in health care. Those decisions, along with my faith have continued to chart the course of my life. At 20 I moved to South Carolina and began volunteering in a gubernatorial campaign that began a lifetime of working on campaigning. I also won my first seat as a committee person. I’ve been a committee person in three states, including the last 16 years in Hightstown. I’ve also been a Republican Club president, municipal chair and Hightstown councilwoman, all the while continuing to volunteer on local and national campaigns. After 30 years of volunteering in the party, it was a natural evolution to choose to run for Assembly after being asked by both of my running mates to join their team.
answers.Why are you running for office?: As previously stated, I have a strong compulsion for public service, I believe I bring a unique and effective skill set and background to Trenton, and I believe people crave representation by people who understand their lived experience. As a health care provider, I will approach legislation like triage. Assess the situation/issue, listen to the people, work with your team and find a diagnosis/legislation to effectively resolve the problem. As an activist and a caregiver, I believe I can work across the aisle, provide good constituent service and effect much-needed change. The most important thing is to put the people over politics.
answers.Key election issue: Education. I believe the issue of parental rights, fair education funding formulas and the greater issue of school choice is the civil rights issue of our time.
answers.Example of a successful project: I, with a little help, began a ministry at my Church that paired young, diverse adults with seniors in nursing homes who didn’t have strong family support and were struggling with loneliness. We built a database and a team of 20 to 30 volunteers who were personally paired with specific members of the elderly community who were matched based on commonalities, like life experience, race and military service. That idea has since been incorporated into a nationwide, nondenominational group called Stephen Ministry. It’s not quite the same, but I’m very proud of the need that I recognized in the senior community and the initiative that it produced.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: I experienced a workplace accident that left me 100% disabled. As someone who has always worked more than one job for the better part of my life, and volunteering as well, it was devastating not only physically, but emotionally. I’ve had to fight my way back through the medical and legal systems. I’ve filled my life with much volunteer work, not just the political. I serve on the Board of Health in Hightstown, been an EMT on my local ambulance squad, done wildlife rehab, 16 years on the Mercer County Medical Reserve Corps, where we responded to floods, fires, emergencies, and most recently the COVID pandemic. I am also a Stephen Minister at my church, which is supremely rewarding, and a validation that any trial we go through in life can in turn be beneficial to someone in our community .
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: I am a strong advocate of the Second Amendment. It is frequently proven that most crimes are not committed by law-abiding citizens. I strongly believe our Constitution allows us much greater rights than we are provided by New Jersey. I believe the recent Bruin case reinforced that, and the Murphy administration is making every effort to work around the Supreme Court and New Jersey citizens who have the right to protect themselves, their families and their businesses. We need to focus on enforcing the laws already on the books and keeping illegal guns out of the hands of criminals. Did I mention my husband says I’m a good shot?
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: I am an all-of-the-above person when it comes to energy. Frankly, I believe Gov. Murphy is rushing headlong into a radical green energy plan that science and our infrastructure does not support. We don’t know exactly why record numbers of whales and dolphins are washing up on our beaches. There are theories, but can we just have a moratorium and an independent study done so we can follow the actual science? Not to mention that wind energy is intermittent at best, and a big hurricane will not only destroy the windmills but will fill our ocean with thousands of gallons of oil and other toxic pollutants. We are rushing mandates on electric vehicles that will financially cripple our middle- and lower-class residents, not to mention people in congregate housing that doesn’t make allowances for chargers, and an electrical grid that certainly can’t support it. Don’t get me started on the unelected BPU-making policy about gas stoves; ask anyone who cooks how they feel about that…
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: This is the question that I struggle the most with in this survey, seriously. Obviously, property in New Jersey is very expensive, coupled with crippling mortgage rates and the highest property taxes around. It doesn’t help that big corporations and venture capitalists are buying up starter homes around the state and charging outlandish rents. There is no reasonable bridge from low-income or subsidized housing to home ownership. All I can say is that one-party rule in Trenton isn’t helping anyone. There are no checks and balances. There has been no positive change in decades of Democratic control. People need to realize this so they don’t continue to perpetuate the same vicious cycle.
answers.Final thoughts: I am what used to be called a compassionate conservative. I know that President Bush caused that term to fall out of favor. I am in this because I care. Due to my disability, I cannot take a salary; there is no avenue of personal gain for me. As an EMT or health care provider, I don’t ask your party affiliation before I take care of you. As an elected official I will do the same. My motto is “Fighting for your Rights and Liberties while caring for the least of these.” That’s who I am, and what you’ll be getting if you vote for me. I am asking for your vote on Nov 7, or earlier if you choose to vote that way.

answers.Plain: Age : 82 Hometown : Lawrence Twp. (Mercer) Occupation : Legislator Personal background : I was born and raised in Dover, New Jersey, before relocating to Trenton to attend The College of New Jersey, formerly known as Trenton State College. I have lived in Mercer County ever since. I am a first-generation college graduate. I earned a B.S. in education from Trenton State College and an M.A. in guidance and counseling from Rider University, formerly known as Rider College. I completed my doctoral credits in education (ABD) at Rutgers University. I worked as a health and physical education teacher in the Trenton school district before being hired by Rider College. There, I worked as the Educational Opportunity Fund counselor and assistant director to economically disadvantaged youth. I also worked as the associate director and director of career services. I am now retired and work as a full-time legislator. I am married and have two children and five grandchildren. Political background : I was the first African American woman to be elected to the Mercer County Board of Freeholders in the 1980s and was elected as vice president of the Freeholder Board in 1986. I served two terms in the New Jersey General Assembly from 1994 to 1998 and as associate minority leader from 1996 to 1998 before being elected to the New Jersey Senate. I served as Senate president pro tempore from 2002 to 2009. I am the first African American to be elected to the New Jersey Senate in the 15th District and the second African American woman to be elected to the New Jersey Senate. I am the first woman and African American to be elected as Senate president pro tempore. Why are you running for office : I enjoy being of service to our community and state. I have set a standard of excellence in constituent services, I pay close attention to the needs and concerns of my constituents, and I have been an effective voice for them in the New Jersey Legislature and, in particular, a voice for the voiceless. Key election issue : The issue of learning recovery since the pandemic remains an important concern. Remote learning led to declines in achievement, especially in school districts with high rates of poverty. I want to ensure that our state is providing the support that our districts and families need to help our students prepare for college, vocational training or the workforce. My bill, S1373, would establish a three-year pilot program in the Department of Education to support school district programs to increase the length of the school day or year in lowest-performing school districts. I have promoted extended school days and school years for many years to help support student learning, provide teachers with extra time for teaching and to help save parents the cost of after-school care or summer camp. I believe a change to our school schedule is long overdue. School schedules should be better aligned with parents’ work schedules. In most families, both parents work and families are spending a fortune in afterschool care and summer camps. Children from families that cannot afford after-school and summer programs are left unattended and at risk of getting into trouble. Additionally, our taxpayers have spent billions of dollars on school buildings that are underutilized, as our students are in school for only 180 days per year and only five or six hours of those days. Teachers often need to find employment to have income for 12 months out of the year, instead of just nine. By extending the school year, teachers will be able to earn more and not be in the position of supplementing their salaries. Other states have modified school schedules and have lengthened the school year, and I believe it is something that should be considered on a more widespread scale in our state than the just the 20 districts that I have proposed in my bill. However, additional instruction time is especially needed now to support learning recovery, which will prevent losing students altogether and causing greater risk of dropping out, joblessness, poverty, poor health and/or criminal behavior. I am also the sponsor of S1590, which establishes the Extended School Day and School Year Study Commission, which would be tasked with studying the effects of a longer school day and school year on advancing student achievement, enhancing the overall school learning environment and increasing student enrichment opportunities and educational offerings. Example of a successful project : I have been in the forefront of advocating for expanding access to affordable contraceptives to promote non-abortion services and help prevent unwanted pregnancies. I believe that access to contraceptives should be the foremost policy to help women achieve their desired family size. I sponsored the law to require health insurers to cover prescription contraceptives for up to 12 months. Access to a 12-month supply helps prevent gaps in birth control use and makes it easier on women. Continuously paying for a visit to the doctor to renew a prescription is costly and an inconvenience for women who are working and juggling their families and other responsibilities. I then successfully passed legislation to permit pharmacists to dispense self-administered hormonal contraceptives to help make it easier and less costly for women to access contraceptives. I am proud of the work that I have accomplished to reduce barriers for contraceptive access and to ensure that women’s reproductive and health care needs are included in our policy making decisions. Example of a challenge faced : I learned a lot from my first political fight when I was a Mercer County freeholder in the 1980s. Before the phrase “environmental justice” became popular, I fought along with my running mate the late Anthony Carabelli, to oppose a garbage incinerator from being built in a neighborhood in the City of Trenton. At the time, the project was supported by the suburban members of the Freeholder Board and county executive, the Chamber of Commerce, the editorial boards of both major newspapers, the trade unions, and all of the mayors in Mercer County, except Trenton Mayor Holland, so we felt very much like lone soldiers. The project would have been a white elephant, bringing huge trucks with garbage through Trenton to burn at the facility located in a densely populated municipality in Mercer County that would have been subjected to toxic pollution. The city was selected because the home values were low, and the project would have cost millions of dollars that would have been wasted spending. The freeholders traveled to Vienna to learn about recycling and as an alternative to the waste incinerator, we recommended that we do more recycling rather than create more pollution. We remained consistent in our position and were unwilling to support the project; as a result, the Freeholder Board did not have the votes needed to approve the project in Trenton. My position cost me reelection. I put people over politics and have no regrets. The experience taught me that you should always follow your convictions, even when you are the only one on that path, and that experience has informed my actions and leadership through the years. On NJ’s gun laws : I am proud to have voted for legislation that has made New Jersey gun laws among the strictest in the country. I would not change our gun laws. However, as long as gun laws in other states and at the federal level remain lax, it is too easy for individuals to purchase guns and bring them across our borders. Our federal background check system needs to be improved with the use of universal background checks. States must report individuals who cannot legally possess a weapon due to crimes or mental illness to ensure that federal background checks are returning accurate information. We must also do more to change young attitudes about the use of gun violence to resolve conflicts and strengthen our mental health system. On the Murphy administration’s climate change proposals : I support efforts to combat climate change, but I am concerned that some decisions are being made from a place of privilege and not a real understanding of the financial hardships and other challenges that our residents and businesses are facing. The high cost of electric vehicles make them unaffordable for low-income and middle class individuals and families. Depending upon the level of electric vehicle, homes may need upgrades for special charging equipment, which is another added cost. We do not have the infrastructure in place to support vehicle charging, including at multiple dwelling developments. We do not know how this type of rule will impact existing businesses or our ability to attract new businesses to our state. Additionally, I am concerned that the cost to replace the battery of an electric vehicle will create another financial strain for people who cannot afford the high cost of a battery. China dominates electric vehicle battery technology and it would be wise to first diversify our supply chain and also ensure that we are not undermining U.S. manufacturers and jobs. I believe that these issues need to be carefully considered before our state issues a ban on gas-powered vehicles. The more we depend on electric vehicles and appliances, the greater the risk that our residents will be impacted by a major outage attributed to a weather-related event. I believe that consumers should still have the option for a hybrid vehicle at the very least and that we should continue incentivizing the purchase of electric vehicles. We may need a program to help lower-income individuals with the upfront costs of purchasing an electric vehicle or generators during power outages. We should continue developing the infrastructure to support electric charging. We need to ensure that our utility companies have solid emergency response plans for restoring electricity, which is already a problem for many communities during weather-related events. On housing affordability and property taxes : The New Jersey Legislature has taken great strides to reduce property taxes and provide more relief to homeowners and tenants. The Homestead Credit was replaced by the ANCHOR program and provided relief to both homeowners and tenants. Under the ANCHOR program, property tax relief increased by 625% in the 15th Legislative District. We also expanded the income eligibility for the senior freeze program from just under $100,000 to $150,000 to allow more senior citizens to freeze their property taxes and be reimbursed for any increase in property taxes they may incur. Finally, we passed the StayNJ program to reduce property taxes by 50 percent for eligible homeowners beginning in 2026. We still need to do more to help make it more affordable for businesses and renters in New Jersey. Since 2000, I have sponsored legislation to allow for a state constitutional convention to reform New Jersey’s system of property taxation. My goal is to make our state more affordable by reducing taxes and reforming the way we pay for schools and government services. We need to be less reliant on property taxes as a form of revenue to pay for education and government. We need a fairer and more progressive form of taxation and we need to consolidate towns and school districts to help reduce taxes and rent. I am the sponsor of S934, which establishes guidelines for creditworthiness determinations concerning affordable housing programs. When a renter has an opportunity to live in an affordable unit, where their rent would not exceed 30% of their income, they can be denied due to poor credit. Many times, individuals and families have been paying market rate rent that is unaffordable, thus creating a situation that negatively impacted their credit. The chance to pay affordable rent would provide the financial relief they need and also lead to significant social benefits; I do not believe it is fair to penalize someone by denying them the opportunity to live affordably. The bill will make affordable housing available to more individuals and families. I also support incentivizing homeownership, especially in high-poverty communities that need more owner-occupied housing to improve the stability of the neighborhood. My bill, S944, establishes the “Police Officer, Firefighter, Public School Teacher, Corrections Officer, and Sanitation Worker Home-Buyer Assistance Act.” The goal is to encourage certain public safety workers and other municipal employees to live in the communities they serve by providing downpayment assistance with 0% interest that would be forgiven at a rate of 20% over five years. The presence of public safety workers would help to improve the safety of neighborhoods, improve the connection public safety officers have in community, and provide positive role models for our children. I am also the sponsor of S3002, which establishes the Residential Property Repair Program, to allow low-interest loans to homeowners or prospective homeowners to fix homes that are in disrepair and make them livable as the applicant’s primary residence. The bill uses existing housing stock to create affordable housing that is decent, safe and secure.

Age : 60 Hometown : Stockton Occupation : Owner/Manager of a geothermal/net zero mechanical company and a large tree nursery Personal background : I was born and live in Stockton, New Jersey. Local schools up through a B.S. in agricultural economics, continued graduate studies in natural resource and environmental economics. I just completed a master’s degree in public administration (MPA) (Pi Alpha Alpha). I have farmed continuously throughout my life – general, vegetables, honey, beef, turkeys, chickens. I milked up to 150 cows, and worked on a dairy grain farm. Started a tree moving company to pay for college. Created a large tree nursery and tried organic grain and poultry for several years. Simultaneously created a construction company that specialize in geothermal, and net zero construction with solar. I also have a master HVACR license, registered municipal clerk, certified public works manager, qualified purchasing agent and affordable housing professional certification for New Jersey. Political background : I started volunteering on the Shade Tree Commission, then the Environmental Commission. I have been on two Municipal Utility Boards and the Planning Board. I was elected to two terms on the Township Committee, two terms as deputy mayor, two terms as mayor, police commissioner. I currently sit on the Board of Trustees at Raritan Valley Community College as the vice chair and finance committee chair. Why are you running for office : I am tired of the stalemate, one party rule of Trenton. The residents’ and taxpayers’ needs are passed over. The Clean Energy Fund is raided, funding is misappropriated. Tax credits are given away to foreign companies. Key election issue : Building back the economy, balancing education costs with outcomes, creating environmentally sound solutions. Education, the economy and the environment are all blended together in a successful, productive New Jersey. We need to focus on educating our youth, adults returning for training and continuing education to be productive members of society. The more members we have contributing to society, the faster the economy grows. There is a tremendous opportunity in the environmental field, there are up to fivefold reductions in energy usage in sourcing heat pumps through ground source applications. Customer-based solar reduces the need for grid expansions. There are square miles of undeveloped roofs in agricultural facilities that would support micro grids of solar production and alternate revenue streams for farmers. Example of a successful project : When I entered the Delaware Township Committee, the Police Department operated out of a trailer. During my terms we built a police facility. I always champion workforce development at RVCC. As a group, we are doing great things there. While others are discussing clean energy, I build net zero homes, I actively convert homes to Home Performance homes. I have written grants, balanced budgets, managed a community through Superstorm Sandy and two other tropical storms and floods. Example of a challenge faced : I am in the biggest challenge of my life. I am learning how to navigate my world from an electric wheelchair. I have adapted my world to be ADA functional. I have always been a champion for access. On NJ’s gun laws : Laws need to address criminals, not law abiding citizens. On the Murphy administration’s climate change proposals : NO. The math is wrong and the timelines are impractical. If they were sincere, no group would be allowed to raid the Clean Energy Fund. Even California is admitting the solutions are at the customers’ site or close to it. Micro grids need to be developed, every large agricultural and commercial rooftop should be explored for solar, every mill race needs to be explored and developed for hydra-electric. Where gas lines cross electric lines, there can be small clean natural gas generators. Most of New Jersey’s electrical generation is either gas or nuclear. It is cheaper and easier to convert to ground source heat pumps. These units provide up to five times reduction in energy demand. No grid expansions, reduction in solar field sizes at the use. What would I do differently? I’d vote no. I think it is bad form for the governor’s former employer to be in charge of the stocks and bond sale for the company installing the wind farm. I would also review the damage to marine life. Not reviewing it is morally wrong. On housing affordability and property taxes : You have to go back to the source. Rent, housing and property taxes are high because school costs are high. Converting schools to solar and geothermal would be a reduction in physical costs. Society determines what level of service is required. From that, those involved must attempt to provide it economically. Originally the state income tax was imposed to help fund school costs. It is a spending crisis. Final thoughts: I believe I bring a unique blend of business and policy background, with a good foundation of math, economics and education. The taxpayer, the environment and education can thrive. Campaign website

Age : 59 Hometown : Pennington Occupation : Retired Personal background : Assemblyman Anthony S. Verrelli has been committed to helping other people his entire life. An unapologetic advocate for New Jersey’s working-class families, he believes that everyone deserves a second chance and an opportunity to succeed. Raised in Trenton and Lawrence by Italian and Scottish immigrants to the United States, graduated from Notre Dame High School before attending the Sam F. Secretario Carpenters Training Center. Anthony became a member of the United Brotherhood of Carpenters & Joiners of America in 1989 and remained a union member for over 35 years. Anthony has been a proud member of the Hopewell Township Knights of Columbus since 2010. Anthony; his wife, Donna; his daughter, Alyssa; and his parents, Georgina and Freddie, live in Pennington, and Anthony’s brother, Ronnie, lives in Ewing. Political background : Anthony served on the Mercer County Board of Chosen Freeholders (now called County Commissioners) from 2016 to 2018 and has served the working families of the 15th Legislative District in the New Jersey General Assembly since August 2018. Assemblyman Verrelli is chair of the Assembly State & Local Government Committee, vice chair of the Assembly Labor Committee, vice chair of the Assembly Community Development & Affairs Committee and a member of the Assembly Special Committee on Infrastructure and Natural Resources. Why are you running for office : I’m running for office to continue the work that I’ve been doing my entire life. Before I was in office, the issues of worker’s rights, improving access to mental health services, addiction/recovery treatment (particularly with the ongoing opioid crisis), and ensuring that people leaving incarceration are given a fair chance at success were still at the forefront of my mind. Furthermore, as we see an evolving labor landscape in New Jersey and throughout this country, we must also ensure that working people have protections that allow them to work safely and with dignity. All of these issues are about improving the quality of life of every resident in New Jersey, whether in my district or not. Key election issue : As I stated above, New Jersey is a state that must be uniquely bold in approaching the challenges that it faces. As the most densely populated state in the country, we have to be. The cost of living is the biggest issue on everyone’s mind, but that cost isn’t just dollars and cents. It’s the cost of the opioid crisis plaguing our communities. It’s the cost of dwindling access to mental health services. And it’s the cost of residents needing legal protections to protect their jobs and livelihoods. These issues are a “cost” of living, and we must address them all from that perspective. Throughout the current legislative session, I have put much effort into pushing forward bills that tackle the issues above. These include A3672, which seeks to eliminate obstacles to harm reduction programs; A3674, aimed at establishing a special probation drug court; AR186, to raise awareness about the dangerous effects of the drug xylazine; and the ANCHOR program, which provided historic property tax relief for over 1.7 million New Jersey residents. I also introduced and sponsored A4772, which grants striking workers access to unemployment benefits, allowing them to advocate for better working conditions. Example of a successful project : As a carpenter by trade, I’ve completed many projects throughout my career, and I’m proud of those successes. As a legislator, navigating a bill from introduction to the governor’s desk for their signature can be best described as the most important project I work on. My legislative work has been successful throughout my term, and there’s no better example than A4772, the UI Strike Bill. This first-in-the-nation bill enables striking or locked-out workers to receive unemployment benefits two weeks into their struggle. If the company hires replacement workers, those benefits start immediately. In a time when workers across America are exercising their collective bargaining rights, this bill could not be more necessary. It required extensive research, conversations with stakeholders, time, and care from introduction to signing. Proudly, it was signed and is now law. And this new law has already helped striking workers to pay their bills and feed their families. Example of a challenge faced : Entering the New Jersey General Assembly as a newly elected assemblyperson is an incredibly challenging experience. To be successful, one must be willing to listen to and learn from those who have come before them. Being a quick learner is crucial, as is being open to having your opinions challenged and being willing to change them. Most of these skills I developed as a carpenter. There was always something to learn from somebody. It’s about serving others and not yourself. On NJ’s gun laws : I’ve always supported sensible gun reform, and the proof is in the legislation I’ve supported. One such example is S3150, which establishes strict-liability criminal penalties for firearm trafficking that results in injury or death. Law enforcement from across the state and Gov. Phil Murphy supported it as a tangible policy that will hopefully stem the tide of gun violence in New Jersey. On the Murphy administration’s climate change proposals : I do. The movement toward a greener future in New Jersey has been steady, fueled by job growth. My labor endorsements exemplify that. Climate change is real, and we can simultaneously boost our economy and greenify our communities. They’re not mutually exclusive. These policies improve the quality of life of all New Jerseyans through a cleaner world and good jobs. I’m proud to support that mission. On housing affordability and property taxes : The issue of housing affordability (whether it be rent, property taxes or anything else) needs to be addressed in more than one way. That is to say, there is no single fix. During my term, I’ve worked diligently to ensure that the new housing we’re building is of a high quality, whether it’s market rate or affordable. I’m pushing for A669 to make getting rental housing easier for people with mixed credit histories. I’ve also protected current residents from being priced out of their homes and neighborhoods. Programs like ANCHOR (which includes renters), the senior property tax freeze program, and Stay NJ all work toward that aim. And I’m proud to have voted in favor of those programs because they’ve made a tangible impact on the residents’ bottom line, and that’s where it counts. Campaign website

Age : 23 Hometown : Trenton Occupation : Cashier Personal background : First generation American on my father’s side (from Colombia), fourth on my mother’s (from Italy). Born and raised in Trenton. Graduate of Mercer County Community College, currently in my senior year at Kean University studying public administration and political science. Parking lot attendant and cashier at the Cure Insurance Arena in Trenton. Candidate for Pi Alpha Alpha and Pi Sigma Alpha honor societies. Member of the Knights of Columbus and the Italian Sons and Daughters of America. Political background : Currently a member of the Mercer County Republican Committee, vice chair of the Trenton Republican Committee, member of the New Jersey Young Republicans State Committee, and chair of the New Jersey College Republicans. Previously ran for Mercer County commissioner in 2021 and managed the successful campaign of Jennifer Williams for Trenton City Council. Why are you running for office : New Jersey needs lawmakers with a new vision, people who know intimately the challenges of life in this rapidly changing economy. For too long our state has been hemorrhaging people and talent. We spend so much educating our children only for them to begin life in another state while those entering retirement do so in another state. New Jersey needs a class of lawmakers not beholden to any particular ideology or political style, we need lawmakers concerned with improving life for our people. Key election issue : School funding, moving away from a property-tax-based formula. It’s unfair to urban schools and keeps property taxes among the highest in the country. Solutions include c ombined school districts with more streamlined administration as well as increasing aid to public schools from the state budget. Example of a successful project : Managed the successful city council campaign for Jennifer Williams, the first openly trans person elected to a municipal council in New Jersey. Assisted in the founding and operation of the Students Against Animal Cruelty club at Kean University. Example of a challenge faced : Getting my degree. While at Mercer I became homeless during the COVID pandemic. I’ve also had to commute every single day to Kean University from Trenton on NJ Transit. I’m very fortunate to have my tuition covered by grants but books, transportation, food and costs at home have made it tough. Nevertheless, I’m committed to getting my bachelor’s degree. On NJ’s gun laws : I’d have to study this issue more carefully but so far the right to bear arms has been protected in New Jersey while also ensuring that we are among the very lowest in gun-related crime. On the Murphy administration’s climate change proposals : Not entirely, I remain opposed to the construction of wind turbines along the shore. On housing affordability and property taxes : Changing our school funding formula will help lower property taxes. For those who hope to own their own home, creating an economy with high-paying jobs and dynamic careers will help people gain a better footing to someday own their own home. For renters, lowering property taxes will also help them. Campaign website

Age : 52 Hometown : Trenton Occupation : Grants administrator Personal background : I was raised in the vibrant and diverse city of Trenton, New Jersey. I am a proud graduate of Trenton Central High School. After high school, I earned a BA in sociology from Trenton State College/The College of New Jersey, an MSA in administration from Central Michigan University, and a certified municipal finance license from Rutgers University, School of Government Services. Before my current role as a grants administrator for Mercer County, I worked at the New Jersey Department of Community Affairs and the Mercer County Board of Social Services. My deep connection to my community and my experience as a social worker for over 20 years has shaped my values and my commitment to public service. Political background : My first ever role as a public servant was as an advocate for my family and loved ones. From there, I eventually became a voice for my city and community as a councilwoman in the capital city of Trenton. I served as a member of the Trenton City Council for almost eight years and then I was given the great opportunity to serve as assemblywoman for the 15th Legislative District. I am the constituent outreach chair for the New Jersey General Assembly. I also serve on the Joint Committee on the Public Schools, the Joint Committee on Economic Justice and the Commerce and Economic Development, Budget, Higher Education and Equal Employment Opportunity committees. Why are you running for office : For most of my adult life, I have tried to live by the words: “If you have something to say, say it, speak up and speak out.” I decided to run because I remember thinking that the system was overwhelming and that the people around me needed an advocate who would work to make the world more equitable, just and accessible. I wanted to create a better world for my nieces and nephews. I wanted to use my voice to advocate for my community members who could not or were not able to advocate for themselves. For those who are working hard but are at a disadvantage in today’s society. I had something to say, and I made it my personal mission to say it, speak up and speak out. I am running for re-election to continue advocating and fighting to create a better world for generations to come. Key election issue : A key issue for me in this election is economic empowerment, particularly in the context of the ongoing economic challenges for working-class families across the state. New Jersey voters deserve policies and initiatives that prioritize their financial well-being, support small businesses and ensure equitable access to economic opportunities. Two areas of economic empowerment that I am particularly interested in are workforce development and access to quality health care, which are crucial to ensuring that every resident has the opportunity to thrive. To address the key issue of economic empowerment, workforce development, and health care access, I have been a strong advocate for practical and impactful solutions that directly benefit the people of New Jersey. Several bills I’ve sponsored and worked on, some of which have become law, reflect my commitment to these critical areas: Economic Empowerment:  Affordable Housing Initiatives: I have supported legislation aimed at expanding access to affordable housing, ensuring that families have stable and affordable homes.  Tax Incentives/Programs: I’ve championed bills to provide tax incentives and resources to residents across the state, to help them weather economic challenges and thrive.  Education Equity: I’ve been at the forefront of efforts to enable students, particularly those in underserved communities, to receive a quality education.  Job Training Initiatives: I’ve supported measures that fund job training and placement programs, helping individuals gain the skills they need for in-demand jobs.  STEM Education: Encouraging STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics) education is a priority. I’ve worked on bills to expand STEM opportunities in our schools.  Maternal Health Initiatives: I’ve supported measures to address maternal health disparities and improve access to prenatal and postpartum care.  Mental Health Parity: I’ve advocated for mental health parity legislation to ensure that mental health services are on par with physical health services. Bills signed into law:  A-998 – Codifies and expands ARRIVE Together Pilot to make certain mental health services available to police responding to certain emergencies; appropriates $2 million.  A-3852 – Establishes New Jersey Child Tax Credit Program  A-5472 – Establishes New Jersey Maternal and Infant Health Innovation Center Act, & and appropriates $2,220,000  A-5672 – Increases child tax credit under gross income tax Example of a successful project : One of the most impactful and rewarding experiences I’ve had the privilege to be a part of was my involvement in the New Jersey Complete Count Commission. Serving on this commission allowed me to play a significant role in ensuring that every resident of our great state had the opportunity to be counted in the U.S. Census. My involvement with the commission also underscores my commitment to preserving our democracy and ensuring that every voice is heard. It was a successful program in its own right, but more important, it was a testament to the power of collective action and the impact we can have when we work together for the common good. Example of a challenge faced : I love learning, but when I got to the Legislature or when I joined the City Council, there was no book or person to guide you through how to do this. There’s a lot to learn to be an effective legislator and oftentimes information is key. There isn’t necessarily a guidebook about how to be an assemblyperson and there are still legislative districts in our state that have never had Black or women state representatives. People often talk about the importance of representation, but we don’t always talk about the challenge of being the first or one of the few. Ultimately, I think it’s important to have a strong support network around you and I was blessed to have people around me who made my transition to the Legislature a little easy. I also had the opportunity to learn from and be mentored by mavericks like Sen. Ron Rice and Lt. Gov. Sheila Oliver. On NJ’s gun laws : New Jersey’s gun laws have been shaped by a strong commitment to public safety and they reflect our dedication to creating safer communities for all residents. As an advocate for responsible gun legislation, I believe that the current laws – including the recently enacted Measures – are important steps toward achieving that goal. I support measures such as universal background checks, restrictions on high-capacity magazines and keeping firearms out of the hands of domestic abusers and those who pose a danger to themselves and others. I also support increased coordination regionally between New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania to help limit regional access to illegal support. On the Murphy administration’s climate change proposals : I wholeheartedly support the Murphy administration’s initiatives to combat climate change, which include the promotion of electric cars and increased use of electricity in new buildings and appliances. These initiatives reflect our commitment to environmental stewardship, sustainable energy and reducing our carbon footprint. While I fully support the Murphy administration’s efforts to combat climate change, my focus would be on making sure we have the workforce for these energy sources, making clean energy solutions affordable for all and ensuring that vulnerable communities are active participants in and beneficiaries of the energy transition. Together, we can create a more sustainable, inclusive and environmentally responsible future for New Jersey. On housing affordability and property taxes : Addressing the cost of rent, housing affordability, and property taxes in New Jersey is a multifaceted challenge that requires comprehensive and innovative solutions. I have been deeply committed to these issues throughout my tenure as an assemblywoman and I’ve championed several bills and initiatives, such as the ANCHOR program and expanding the Child Tax Credit, that are aimed at making a positive impact on the lives of our residents. To further address the challenges of housing affordability and property taxes, I believe in continuing to:  Strengthen Rent Control Laws: Ensuring that rent control laws are fair to both tenants and landlords is essential.  Explore Property Tax Reform: We need to explore comprehensive property tax reform that addresses the structural issues causing high property taxes in our state.  Landlord Accountability: It’s imperative that we hold landlords accountable for providing safe and quality housing. Final thoughts: Empowerment is at the heart of creating opportunities for the next generation. As an assemblywoman, I am deeply committed to ensuring that our youth have access to mentorship, internships, career exposure and the overall support they need to thrive. My dedication to creating opportunities for the next generation stems from my belief in the potential of our youth. When we support and show up for them, we can empower them to reach their full potential and contribute to a stronger, more prosperous New Jersey for all. Campaign website

answers.Political background: I became the first Democrat to represent the 16th District when I was elected as an assemblyman in 2015. Since then, I have used my position to advocate for expanding access to voting, clean energy infrastructure, gun safety reform and making New Jersey a more affordable place to raise a family. I was elected to the Senate in 2021.
answers.Why are you running for office?: I have found that my science background gives me a unique perspective in the Legislature and helps to bring new, innovative ideas to the body. I would be honored to continue to represent the people of my community in Trenton.
answers.Key election issue: Ensuring all students have the freedom to access learning materials, women have the freedom to decide their own health care, and families have the ability to afford to live in the community where they work.
answers.Example of a successful project: For 18 years I was the head of the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory’s (PPPL) Science Education Program, which was focused on providing opportunities for those traditionally underrepresented in the STEM fields. Currently, I am the head of strategic partnerships at PPPL and focused on public-private collaborations to accelerate the development of fusion energy.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: Moving from science to politics was one of the most challenging professional endeavors that I’ve ever attempted. To state the obvious, science and politics are typically not combined, but I think they are a wonderful combination. Like anything else, it takes dedication and focus to learn and improve, and I hope I’ve gotten a little bit better each and every day.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: In my time in the NJ Legislature, I have been a leading voice for gun safety legislation. I co-sponsored S1204, requiring the registration of handguns purchased out of state, and sponsored or voted for every other gun safety legislation in front of me, including requiring reporting of large purchases of ammunition, strengthening criteria for obtaining a handgun permit, and requiring gun manufacturers to follow procedures that make tracking weapons easier. Because of my leadership in Trenton, I was recently named a Moms Demand Action Gun Sense Candidate.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: I have spent my entire professional career working on the development of fusion energy — clean, safe, carbon-free and nearly unlimited electricity once it is completed. I support the Murphy administration’s goal of making NJ a leader in state-level initiatives to reduce our carbon footprint. Incentivizing the transition to carbon-free energy as quickly as possible is key, and I’d like to see an increased investment in electric vehicle rebates and electrification efforts.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: One of my recent accomplishments in the Legislature is the passage of the StayNJ bill, which reduces property taxes for seniors, allowing them to stay in their communities and with their families. I would continue to support measures that reduce the property tax burden on NJ residents.

answers.Personal background: Entrepreneur and electrical engineer (BSEE, MSEE) with hardware design, software and management experience. Inventor listed on 16 issued US patents. US Army Vietnam veteran. Former NJ emergency medical technician. IEEE senior life member. Volunteer Hillsborough Rescue Squad, VFW and VVA life member; volunteer adviser for American Corporate Partners (acp-usa.org).
answers.Political background: Was Somerset County Republican Organization representative for Hillsborough Voting District 2 – won with one write-in vote during the primary election – not really a public office.
answers.Why are you running for office?: Was displeased that the Libertarian Party and Green Party candidates were not allowed to participate in the presidential debates, preventing serious candidate deficiencies from being brought up. Personally, I don’t feel that people who I consider to be draft evaders should become commanders in chief. A question that neither of those two candidates wanted to bring up.
answers.Key election issue: NJ should keep its nose out of people’s business.
answers.Example of a successful project: East Powelton Concerned Residents: participated in a Neighborhood Historical Renovation Pilot Program to renovate three buildings. Was responsible for rehabilitating one of these first three. All three were renovated successfully. Saved these 19th century urban buildings in neighborhood from being demolished, created low-income apartments. Subsequently, many of the other beautiful century-old buildings in the East Powelton, Philadelphia, urban neighborhood followed in historical rehabilitation and were also saved.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: My father died at a young age, leaving my mother with five children, one an infant and another with Down syndrome. Growing up in a single-parent family was a challenge, so we all had to scrimp, work and care for each other in order to survive.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: Repeal! The right to bear arms shall not be abridged.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: Probably liquid hydrogen storage as being developed in Australia is better than lithium ion battery storage and EVs. Especially as NJ is a coastal state.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: The free market.
answers.Final thoughts: Byrne’s experience as a veteran, volunteer emergency responder, engineer and inventor will bring useful talents and possibly novel solutions to the NJ Senate.

answers.Personal background: I attended State University of New York–Oneonta and Brunel University of London. Before I was a legislator, my professional career was in business. The majority of my private-sector career was with Prudential Financial, holding several positions leading strategy and analytic teams.
answers.Political background: I was originally elected to the Legislature in 2017, becoming only the second Democrat to represent Legislative District 16. This election was my first run for political office (aside from active involvement in college student government, many years prior).
answers.Why are you running for office?: I am running for reelection because I believe New Jersey is a great place to live and raise a family. I believe that the government’s primary function is to improve the lives of our communities, and to focus upon a family’s future. This is done most effectively when the government works together, when all levels of government, and all parties, work to lift people up instead of pointing fingers for failings. I want to ensure that all New Jerseyans have the opportunity to thrive and can afford to stay in their communities throughout their lives.
answers.Key election issue: My key issue in this election and beyond is making New Jersey a safe and affordable place to raise a family. We have worked toward this by cutting property taxes for seniors and capping the cost of life-saving medications.
answers.Example of a successful project: I am proud to be a prime sponsor of new legislation that has made major changes, lowering the costs of prescription drugs. Access to health care should never be a matter of economics.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: I have been challenged by negativity and pessimism in political discourse, and I wanted to work with my staff to combat those feelings. So with my team, I work to highlight a minimum of 100 community members each week to thank them for their contributions to the community. From recognizing Girl Scout troop bridging ceremonies to congratulating long-standing community activists, we send personalized letters and Assembly citations to uplift community members and acknowledge the good work they do.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: In my time in the Legislature, I have proposed legislation to increase the minimum age for obtaining a weapons license, as well as sponsored red-flag legislation.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: I support the administration’s energy plan of transitioning away from fossil fuel to renewable energy sources. I strongly support incentive programs that help residents and businesses implement electric choices for transportation, HVAC, appliances, etc.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: In the past few years, the NJ Legislature has implemented the ANCHOR rebate program for both homeowners and renters. This year, the Legislature passed a historic property tax rebate program, StayNJ, which will help to cut property taxes by up to 50% for senior homeowners.

answers.Personal background: I attended Rutgers University, where I was an Eagleton Institute of Politics undergraduate associate, and I live in Raritan Township with my husband, Michael Drulis, and our daughter.
answers.Political background: I started my career as a legislative aide for then assemblyman, now state senator, Bob Smith. I went on to become chief of staff for Assemblyman Joe Egan, serving for over a decade, and then served as district director for congressman Tom Malinowski until January of 2023.
answers.Why are you running for office?: I am running for the opportunity to continue to serve my community and bring my unique perspective as a public servant, small business owner and mother to Trenton.
answers.Key election issue: A key issue for me in this election is safeguarding women’s contraceptive health-care access.
answers.Example of a successful project: I am very proud of my work as district director. I set up and led the congressman’s constituent services program, which helped over 11,600 constituents obtain their federal benefits such as veterans benefits, Social Security payments, tax refunds, SBA assistance and more, recovering over $105 million for constituents in the last year alone. And I did this while also working collaboratively with the congressman and his legislative director to identify needed community projects in the district, as well as other areas of need that resulted in over $9.6 billion in federal funding for the 7th Congressional District during his time in office.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: Like it was for every NJ small business owner, COVID was the ultimate challenge. Due to the nature of the business my husband and I own, we were one of the first groups to be shut down and one of the last sectors to reopen. During the shutdown, we of course were worried about staff members, their health and financial situations. My husband and I made sure to check in on them regularly to see if they needed anything, see how they were doing and if we could be of any help.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: I am proud to live in a state that has passed common-sense gun legislation such as background checks, extreme risk orders (red-flag laws) and secure storage laws that keep our kids and our communities safe, and I will continue to support these gun safety initiatives in office.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: I support the administration’s climate initiatives and would continue to do so in Trenton in a way that is responsible and makes it affordable for NJ families and small businesses to access and utilize these programs.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: NJ has some of the best schools in the nation, and I am a strong supporter of public education. School funding is currently the highest percentage of the local property tax bill and has a direct effect on the cost of rent that landlords charge tenants and monthly mortgage payments with escrow for property taxes. We need to look at the school funding formula and how the state aid is distributed to our districts to ensure that our kids and our schools have the resources they need to be successful and we are not overly relying on property taxes to fund our schools.
