answers.Personal background: I am an environmental advocate and mother of four living in Jefferson Township, where my husband and I have been since 2005. I graduated from Montclair State University. I worked in the corporate world for years, pursuing activist work on the side, until the birth of my daughter, at which point the cost of childcare for an infant and two young boys was so high it didn’t make sense to continue. I have been working full time as a candidate or campaign manager alternately for the last few years, and nearly full time on volunteer projects.
answers.Political background: Although I didn’t start out with a desire to run for office, I’ve been an advocate for political causes for years. Eventually, I couldn’t shake what I had seen and felt compelled to be more directly involved in efforts to combat polluters and build a clean energy economy. I’m a steering committee member of the Jersey Renews coalition, and have been a member of the New Jersey NAACP Environment and Climate Justice team for a couple of years. I am the organizer of Jefferson Township Pride, and have been doing that for four years. I was on the steering committees for the New Jersey March for Science and the New Jersey People’s Climate Movement in 2018. I am the former environmental director at Action Together New Jersey and was an early organizer with NJ 11th for Change. I am the former chair of the Jefferson Township Democratic Committee, having served as chair for five years before passing the baton to new leaders in June.
answers.Why are you running for office?: I am an environmental advocate, a grassroots organizer and a mother of four running to build the clean energy economy, protect health care privacy, access and autonomy, fight for clean air and water, and lead with empathy and fiscal sense. In this time when 20 states have rescinded or banned reproductive health care, I will work to ensure our essential rights remain ours. I also want the job growth, new revenue and exponential economic gains of the booming renewable energy market to thrive here, provide fulfilling well-paying jobs for New Jersey residents, and benefit New Jersey both in terms of revenue and a cleaner environment.
answers.Key election issue: Although what compelled me to run for office in the first place was the urgency of climate action and a just transition to a clean energy economy, I have recently been redistricted into District 25 and am just as appalled by my new senator’s votes as I was by the former. Remarkably, not only do his votes come across as disrespectful toward women but even hateful. He voted No on S49 to codify reproductive health care rights into New Jersey law, but it didn’t stop there. He also signed onto bill S673, which would give fetal tissue full legal personhood, criminalize abortion and jail doctors who perform abortion services for 30 years, and impose mandatory reporting on their staff with jail or fines for noncompliance. He voted No on A3974 to protect women who come to New Jersey for reproductive health care from states where it’s now illegal from being extradited and prosecuted in those states. To want women prosecuted for their health care choices is horrifying to me. He is currently the Senate minority leader and has an outsized ability to impact legislation in New Jersey. Someone who not only opposes women’s rights but wants women prosecuted for exercising those rights has no place in our statehouse. I hope to replace him in the State Senate seat for District 25 and become the first woman elected to the seat.
answers.Example of a successful project: During my time with NJ 11th for Change and then with Action Together New Jersey, I wanted to create free public educational events that would help the general public understand the climate issues we are facing in years to come, and potential solutions for those issues. We have the technology to solve many of these problems; what’s missing sometimes is the political will. My teams and I set up free public forums, both in person and online via livestream, to help people hear from scientists, politicians, advocates and more on environmental issues ranging from clean water, to forestry, to fossil fuel subsidies, to wind energy proposals. I then took it further and set up events with members of Congress as live, livestreamed town halls, so that people could ask their questions directly and hear their questions answered.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: One of the hardest things about running for office is seeing firsthand the barriers that exist in the way of working-class representation. The political system isn’t designed for working-class candidates to break through and serve their districts. For example, candidates can donate to their own political campaigns. This is fantastic for those who can self-fund races with large donations or loans, but a barrier for the working class. From the start, we have to work so much harder just to achieve fundraising levels that are competitive. Similarly, it’s hard for mothers to run. Studies show that most politically inclined women wait until their children are grown to consider candidacy; however, mothers of children under age 18 are great on legislation affecting working families, including everything from childcare to school funding to tax fairness. We need more in office, not less. After Liuba Grechen Shirley won the Federal Election Commission decision to allow federal races to use campaign funds for childcare, I actively joined the fight for campaign funds for childcare in New Jersey, and wrote letters, made calls, organized support and testified in support of Sen. Ruiz’s bill S698 that allowed parents running for office to expense the cost of a babysitter to their political campaigns, paying with money they raise themselves. Bill S698 passed in August 2020. I will continue to support measures that help working class people run for office.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: New Jersey residents deserve to be safe from gun violence – at minimum to the fullest extent practicable under federal and state laws. The gun lobby maintains such a stranglehold on federal representation that we can’t even get common-sense legislation through Congress like background checks for gun sales, which 97% of Americans support. Here in New Jersey, we have some of the safest gun laws in the country, including recent legislation creating a capacity to hold gun manufacturers and dealers accountable for misconduct in the sale and distribution of firearms. At the time of this response, there are no instances of the attorney general making use of the capacity to hold gun distributors accountable for selling highly lethal weapons to gun traffickers or straw purchasers. However, it’s important that layers of accountability are available for such conduct and I support the law being on the books.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: I think science-advised policy remains imperative in any state government. Where the clean energy transition is concerned, it’s critical that we take measures to protect our citizenry from the worst projected climate impacts as outlined by worldwide scientists. Consequential decisions yet to come will require a sense of urgency and of shared purpose. The Murphy administration is working to make sure New Jersey is at the forefront of implementing clean energy systems. I do have some concerns, but on the whole, I support a robust clean energy economy and new jobs for our state. Nationally, the government is seeing approximately seven dollars of private investment to match every dollar of government investment in clean energy; poll after poll shows energy workers want to transition to green jobs, and private companies are greening up their energy sourcing as well. I support the financing, education, training, supply chain work, and manufacturing to enable them to do so. My opponent, on the other hand, votes against these initiatives, including RGGI, which brought $152.2 million into New Jersey last year alone for clean energy investments. He is trying to spin a narrative about clean energy being unaffordable, meanwhile he’s voting against the funding mechanisms, benchmarks and standards, and collaboration to get the work done.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: New Jersey residents and their representatives have to be able to have conversations about taxes. Taxes are how the government pays its bills. We have the best schools, best teachers, best first responders and more in this state, and it’s important that we work to pay our obligations to them, including but not limited to making full pension payments every year. We can’t afford representatives who lack the political courage to look at revenue streams and evaluate their effectiveness; which is to say, when employed New Jersey residents are relying on food pantries to get by, we have a serious affordability problem on our hands. The Child Tax Credit is one way we can put more money back in the hands of working families, and so are the ANCHOR tax rebates, but we also need to look at tax fairness. We shouldn’t make working families pay more than their fair share so that the wealthiest people among us can have tax breaks. We should make permanent the 2.5% tax on mega-corporations enacted during the pandemic rather than reversing it. We should re-evaluate some of the Christie-era tax cuts on high-end luxury items, and consider whether we can still afford to leave those in place. Where my concern in tax conversations is helping working families, my opponent is the opposite. He voted against ANCHOR rebates, against the millionaires’ tax and against corporate taxes.
answers.Final thoughts: District 25 has never elected a woman to the New Jersey State Senate. I am grateful to be a candidate in this district and to have the opportunity, should the voters choose me on November 7, to represent the people from among the people. It would also be wonderful to be the first woman to hold the seat!

answers.Personal background: I am a magazine and digital journalism professional, and a four-time editor in chief, including for Consumer Reports, Prevention and Ladies’ Home Journal. Before that, I held senior editorial roles at Good Housekeeping and Glamour. I have also recently become an adjunct university professor. Over my career in magazine journalism, I focused on creating high-quality, mission-based journalism aimed at improving people’s lives through community and policy change. I specialized in coverage of urgent social issues, including the prevention of gun violence, food and water safety, women’s health care, funding for hospital emergency rooms, sexism in judicial decisions, insurance bias among people of color, the lack of supplement regulation, teen suicide, drunken driving and more. I have interviewed three U.S. presidents and first ladies. My work was twice nominated for a prestigious American Society of Magazine Editors Award and has won multiple editorial awards, including a National Citizens’ Coalition Public Service Award and American College of Emergency Physicians Journalism of Excellence award. I was awarded the “W” award for innovation from YWCA and was named a Folio: 40 Industry Leaders with Impact, and was given the Athena Award from Columbia University for commitment to high-quality health journalism. I also led digital consumer product innovation at Lee Enterprises, the country’s third-largest chain of news sites. I have also been vice president and publisher of Broadway Books, a division of Crown/Random House, publishing titles in narrative non-fiction, current affairs, and memoir. I have a master’s degree from New York University and a bachelor’s degree from Penn State University. I grew up in Queens and moved to New Jersey 35 years ago. I have lived in Madison, New Jersey, for 27 years. My father was a New York City police officer and my mother was an office worker. I am the first person in my family who went to college.
answers.Political background: In my roles as editor in chief of Consumer Reports, Prevention and Ladies’ Home Journal, my advocacy coverage of social issues intersected with congressional policymaking and even political rallies. I also have personally interviewed three sitting U.S. presidents, first ladies, senators, congresspeople, ambassadors and mayors, giving me the opportunity to discuss the concerns of millions of readers – which is not unlike advocating on behalf of one’s constituency. As I engage in my first run for political office, I want to work to ensure that the concerns of citizens in LD25 are being heard – and acted on. I am a lifelong registered Democrat.
answers.Why are you running for office?: As a nearly 30-year resident of New Jersey, a member of the LGBTQ community and a daughter helping to care for my elderly mom, I am concerned about and affected by many of the policy conversations happening in our statehouse around tax fairness, senior care and human rights. I am keenly interested in helping New Jersey build a green economy with strategic investments in solar and wind power, as well as innovations in alterna-plastics; protecting bodily autonomy rights and health care privacy between doctors and patients; protecting LGBTQ rights and safety; safeguarding the learning environment for all students; and protecting our communities from gun violence. I am at a point in my life where I feel moved to make a difference in my district and my state. I want to be part of a new group of elected officials committed to bringing integrity, honesty and transparency to public office. I want to deeply participate in the hard work of democracy. This is government by the people, and I now want to be not just an involved citizen, but an involved public official.
answers.Key election issue: I want to make New Jersey an excellent place for new retirees and seniors to thrive, by advocating for creative, thoughtful and affordable living and housing options that will ensure greater cross-generational benefits in our neighborhoods. We need to put our best minds together – businesses, health care professionals, nutritionists, gerontologists, land use experts – to innovate and build intergenerational co-housing options. As we think about future town planning, I would love to see more mentorship opportunities made easily available to our seniors as well, such that they can share their knowledge with students, be available as resources and friends, and experience the health benefits of having young people regularly present. I am also deeply concerned about the incumbents in our district. They stand against so many matters of decency and freedom. All you need to do is look at their voting records to be genuinely alarmed by their positions. I don’t believe they represent the majority of the voters of LD25, and therefore they should be replaced.
answers.Example of a successful project: During my time as editor in chief of Consumer Reports, our organization reported extensively on – among many other issues – -PFAs (“forever chemicals”) in water, racial bias in auto insurance pricing, violations of consumer data privacy, distracted driving dangers and deaths of babies due to use of inclined baby sleepers, inadequate protection for back seat passengers in cars and test crash dummies that don’t reflect the realities of women’s bodies. In all cases, our sustained investigative reporting resulted in bans of unsafe products, improved water regulations, reform in auto insurance pricing, increased data privacy awareness and protection and innovations in car safety on many fronts. This was all possible due to the dissemination of accurate information to concerned citizens and public officials, and holding authorities accountable. I know I can accomplish the same in Trenton.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: Every senior citizen who enters the health care system needs an advocate. My 90-year-old mother has been in ERs, hospitals, acute care institutions and assisted living respite centers on and off for the last 10 years. These experiences are harrowing, confusing, emotionally and physically exhausting – and expensive. I was able to advocate well for my mother because of my health journalism background, which allowed me to speak fluently with doctors, nurses and social workers. It meant I had the skills to research the best facilities possible. It meant that I knew how to spot trouble brewing in mother’s care, and effectively insist on redress. I also enjoyed a flexible work schedule and a supportive brother and life partner. But I know that not every person has these advantages. We must make the health care industrial complex more navigable for the average senior, so that they are not terrorized and ill served in their moments of greatest need. Given that ten thousand people turn 65 each day, we urgently need sustained and thoughtful reform in this area.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: We need to have sensible gun laws, meaning that there need to be gun-free public zones and rigorous vetting of who can buy and own guns. As the daughter of a New York City police officer, I feel that our police should not be outgunned by criminals carrying assault weapons. Responsible gun owners are in favor of sensible oversight, not unlike the oversight we have of people we entrust to drive cars. Additionally, we need to address gun trafficking. This is an issue I covered in my magazine life going back to the 1990s, when then-Mayor Bloomberg was an early and robust leader on this issue. The recent legislation passed in New Jersey to stop firearms trafficking by increasing penalties for trafficked guns used in crimes, and expressly allowing prosecutors to charge out-of-state gun traffickers, will help keep New Jerseyans safe. I would have voted Yes on this bipartisan legislation.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: Yes, I do support the current Democratic initiatives to combat climate change. We need to:
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: Over the decades, as tax structures created extreme wealth for some and extreme challenges for others, we have lost sight of the ideal that everyone should be able to work one honest job, come home to a safe living space and food to eat, and eventually retire from working with the ability to remain in their homes and communities. I would support tax fairness initiatives that would help the state meet its revenue needs without breaking the backs of working families, the poor, or our retirees. In particular, I’m interested in examining the series of tax cuts on luxury items for the super wealthy and on corporations. Communities are enriched together when all generations support one another, and we make that more possible by letting them keep more of their earnings.
answers.Final thoughts: Over my career, I have been inspired by the power of authentic collaboration between elected officials and motivated citizens, on issues ranging from food safety, hospital funding, women’s health care, prevention of gun violence, and more. I believe I have the skills, drive and commitment to make a difference.

answers.Personal background: I am a family medicine physician, community volunteer and father of two living in Randolph Township, where my wife and I have been since 2013. I graduated from Harvard College with a degree in biology, followed by a doctor of osteopathic medicine degree from Rowan-Virtua School of Osteopathic Medicine, and then a master’s in public administration from Rutgers University. Professionally, I provide primary care and musculoskeletal specialty care in Morristown, New Jersey, where I have been working in resident education, teaching the next generation of family doctors since 2013. I also volunteer locally with the Boy Scouts of America organization as a cubmaster and assistant scoutmaster for the last seven years, as well as multiple national medical organizations where I chair several committees dedicated to education, research and professional achievement.
answers.Political background: While I never really had political ambitions, I found inspiration in caring for many of my patients, who had severe limitations in their ability to get the medications, tests and see the specialists they needed due to excessive prior authorizations and insurance plan limitations. Advocating one patient at a time didn’t make sense, and I considered how I could make a bigger impact for people across the state. I joined and now serve on the executive committee for the New Jersey Association of Osteopathic Physicians and Surgeons, where we aggressively advocate for patients and physicians in New Jersey, and while we made some progress, it didn’t give me the direct access to make change for the state.
answers.Why are you running for office?: I am a primary care physician, medical educator and father who recognized that the chips are stacked against many people when it comes to accessing the health care they need. Even with insurance, red tape and excessive delays keep health out of reach for many. I am running to help reduce the red tape, empower patients and make sure that health care decisions stay where they belong, between a patient and their doctor. I am also running to ensure that New Jersey residents can afford to stay in the state, even after retiring, by working to streamline tax policy and improve efficiency of public services to reduce costs. I also believe that corporations should pay their fair share, rather than getting a free lunch at New Jersey residents’ expense.
answers.Key election issue: I am running to make sure that individual freedoms are maintained. For my patients, I fight to ensure that they are able to access necessary health care, including reproductive health care. I am running to ensure that every person continues to have self-determination and autonomy in this state, and keep the government out of peoples’ health care decisions. I am running to ensure that we maintain our First Amendment freedom of expression and identity. All of these different issues really stem from the issue of government overreach, efforts to insert government into our most personal decisions, violate our privacy and steal our autonomy.
answers.Example of a successful project: In 2013, I began working in Morristown and helped found the family medicine residency program. We designed this brand-new program to provide excellent training in primary care for outpatient and inpatient care, chronic disease management, and care for people across generations. Over the last ten years, we have not only grown, but provide exceptional patient care while also educating our residents. Our program has adapted to expand pediatric access, incorporated a collaborative care model for behavioral health, established a home visit program, developed a musculoskeletal medicine residency program, and pioneered regenerative medicine injections in the region. Establishing such diverse programs required listening to patients, identifying community needs, working with stakeholders, and a fair amount of grit to navigate unexpected challenges, like providing in-person care during a global pandemic.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: People often expect physicians to live a comfortable life, but the reality is that medical school is very expensive, and that students often borrow incredible sums of money to pay for their education without a way to make money. My wife had our first child in my third year of medical school, and the second when I was an intern, making barely enough to pay the mortgage, car payments, loan payments, and still make ends meet. As a working-class child, I didn’t have a trust fund or even a college fund to fall back on, and even while working a second job during my residency, we struggled a lot. With two children under 3, daycare was unaffordable, and we had no local family support to help with child-care.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: New Jersey residents deserve to be safe from gun violence, and fortunately, we enjoy some of the safest firearm regulations in the country. Widely supported red flag laws, background checks and clearance to obtain a firearm purchaser ID card are effective safeguards we can use to keep firearms out of the hands of those who would do harm to others. Unfortunately, firearm ownership is not monitored in an ongoing way. I see patients lose decision-making capacity due to medical conditions all of the time, but there is not a clear process to monitor whether they have access to firearms, or to share that information with authorities. If a patient has a seizure, and may not be safe to drive, the RMV is automatically notified, and people need to recertify that they are safe to resume driving. Unfortunately, there is no parallel for firearm ownership. Red flag laws are reactive, and rely on someone reporting a concern for enforcement.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: I believe that a responsible transition to renewable energy is an important aspect of addressing climate change, and that as a state, we should ensure residents and local governments exploit opportunities for subsidies for choosing renewable energy options when replacing HVAC, appliances or updating their homes. The frequent record-breaking natural disasters, including the horrible air quality this summer, makes it clear that definitive and urgent action is necessary.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: New Jersey residents should be able to have meaningful conversations with their elected representatives about taxes. While taxes generate the resources to pay its bills and finance the public services we enjoy like first responders, road maintenance, excellent schools, and public spaces, we need a balance to ensure those funds are being spent responsibly and with a focus on outcomes. Finances should also anticipate future expenses, including fully funding pensions to support our vital public workers.
answers.Final thoughts: Increasingly, health care is being wrestled with in legislatures across the country, and currently insurance companies hold the power, not patients. With so many health related issues at stake, electing a physician to the Legislature will add a unique perspective, who better to improve health care in New Jersey than a physician who has spent his career fighting red tape and insurance companies for his patients?

answers.Personal background: John Von Achen is an experienced Supply Chain leader in the biotech/pharma industry. Currently leading the North America supply chain and a member of the global supply chain leadership team for Ascensia Diabetes Care in Parsippany, New Jersey.
answers.Political background: As a Democratic Party member, Von Achen has been a candidate for Town Council and county commissioner. Over the years, he has supported multiple campaigns, knocking on doors, providing counsel and as the campaign treasurer. He serves on the Planning Board in Parsippany and was previously chairperson.
answers.Why are you running for office?: The Supreme Court has made it clear over the last few years that states need to establish their own rules for governing; the federal government has a limited role. New Jersey residents need to protect their rights within our own state laws and to ensure democracy is preserved.
answers.Key election issue: He is committed to:
answers.Example of a successful project: I was a principal in the distribution of key materials during COVID-19. I developed the distribution strategy and algorithms to ensure product supported hot spots and surging demand. My work ensured that even with shortages we maintained 95% in stock around the country.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: No matter what your politics are, democracy is essential. Voting is essential.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: I would seek out ways to ensure our gun laws remain the strongest in the United States while tweaking them to avoid interference from the federal government. I would also work with neighboring state legislatures to ensure our bubble of protection created by neighboring states with reasonable gun laws remains intact.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: I think Murphy is on a good path. I would encourage more development of new nuclear (SMR, SFR and thorium).
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: I would encourage more county-based services to ease the burden for municipalities and cut out unnecessary administrative costs. This is something I was pushing for when I ran for county commissioner. Shared services is a Band-Aid many municipalities are implementing on their own, but we can help make things more efficient.

answers.Plain: Age : 43 Hometown : Montclair Occupation : Businessman Personal background : Michael D. Byrne is president of the consulting firm Pilgrim Strategies LLC, proprietor of a pruning business in Montclair, and chairman of the Montclair Republican County Committee Inc. Raised in Montclair where he still resides, Byrne attended Seton Hall Prep and graduated from Montclair High School. He earned a B.A. in liberal arts from Thomas Aquinas College in Santa Paula, California. Political background : I am an independent-minded Republican seeking reform of the New Jersey political system. Insiders in both parties use the power of the “party line” to marginalize candidates who don’t take orders from the unelected power brokers who pull the strings. Earlier this year, I filed an amicus brief in the U.S. Supreme Court urging the court to review Mazo v. Way – a critical case that centers on the deprivation of free speech rights under the party-line, ballot access laws of our state. Why are you running for office : Our Republican Party leaders failed us by not having any candidates on the primary election ballot. They came up short exactly when Republicans should have fielded 120 nominees across the state committed to ending the Murphy administration’s war on families and parental rights. When I saw the primary election sample ballots had no Republican nominees for Senate or Assembly in our district, I recruited running mates who would represent our party and fight for families. Key election issue : Nothing is more important than the integrity of the family. Phil Murphy’s administration is suing multiple school districts to ban them from involving parents in the most sensitive aspects of their childrens’ lives. Instead of welcoming and valuing the love parents have for their children, Murphy’s policies are an all-out assault on the integrity of the family unit. 81% of New Jersey parents – including 61% of Democrats – think Murphy and his allies in the Legislature are wrong to undermine parental rights. A disproportionately high number of gubernatorial appointments to the administration, the courts, and countless government agencies come through Essex County. As a state senator residing in Essex County, I will leverage the power of senatorial courtesy to stop every single appointment Phil Murphy tries to make until he ends his war on local school boards, parents and children. Example of a successful project : From 2005 through 2010, I volunteered for The Writers’ Room at Glenfield Middle School and from 2009 through 2012, I served on the Mayor’s School Board Advisory Committee helping interview and select members of the then-appointed Board of Education. In 2011, I was appointed to the Montclair Municipal Election Review Commission and chosen as its secretary. And from 2011 to 2019, I served as the 27th general chairman of the St. Patrick’s Day Parade Committee in Newark, creating a brand new high school band competition to highlight Music in Our Schools Month. Example of a challenge faced : I have fought for election transparency in Essex County despite significant obstacles. In 2021, 12 Republican votes were lost in Montclair’s Ward 3 District 4 and the election was certified without them. The Board of Elections was represented by the attorney general in court and succeeded in concealing how and why the votes were lost. In 2022, the Board of Elections refused to provide the cure list of voters whose ballots had not been accepted but still could be. I sued for access and got it. The same year, Essex County was the only county in New Jersey not to provide a detailed audit of election results, which I highlighted in the press. Most recently, I exposed the county clerk as having falsely awarded Line A to the Democratic Party 17 years in a row in a supposedly “random” drawing. An hour after we appeared in court, the Republican Party was given Line A. On NJ’s gun laws : The Constitution is clear: Americans have a constitutional right to protect themselves. Twenty-seven states allow permitless carry and 45 states have far simpler rules for exactly how and where firearms can be carried. New Jersey’s system is grossly onerous and undermines the civil liberties of law-abiding Americans. I would sponsor preemption legislation to bar counties and municipalities from passing a “patchwork” of confusing and conflicting local laws that would inadvertently ensnare well-meaning gun owners in the legal system – especially “people that live in Paterson and Newark and Elizabeth and Camden.” On the Murphy administration’s climate change proposals : No. Murphy’s heavy-handed, central-planning approach ignores the burdensome cost of electric vehicles for families who have seen their real wages decline thousands of dollars since their 2019 peak. Moreover, he proposes adding an incredible increase in demand to the electric grid without any plan for guaranteeing adequate supply. Worst of all, Murphy has directed over a billion taxpayer dollars to Orsted, a foreign developer that is now backtracking on its commitment and may abandon its project entirely. Murphy’s policies are nothing more than a series of regressive, hidden taxes that hurt the most vulnerable among us. On housing affordability and property taxes : The Abbott Court decision governing school funding has failed generations of children – both those it was supposed to help in 31 select districts – and those who were denied opportunities in the remainder of the state because so many taxpayer dollars were drained from them. Even worse, as early as 2005, a study by the State Supreme Court acknowledged that half of the poorest children in the state lived outside of the Abbott Districts to begin with! Yet the lopsided system has been perpetuated because political bosses demand that the unfair funding continue to flow regardless of bona fide need or results. In reforming school funding, the money should follow the child, not the ZIP code. Final thoughts: I will sponsor legislation to term-limit assemblymen and state senators to 10 years in each office with a maximum combined service of 18 years to curb the abuse of our pension system. Campaign website

Age : 47 Hometown : Montclair Occupation : Senior partner at the BGill Group, LLC Personal background : I was born in Colombia, immigrated to the United States when I was 14 years old. Graduated from Long Branch High School and then went on to Rutgers University in Newark, where I graduated with a bachelor’s degree with a double major in sociology and Latin American literature. My first job out of college was with NJN (NJ Public Television Station) on a show called Images/Imagenes. I worked for U.S. Rep. Steven Rothman for seven years in the district office, where I served in various roles, including as the director of constituent services. in 2016-17 I served as the co-director of the Latino Outreach Program for gubernatorial candidate Phil Murphy. In 2018 my husband and I founded the BGill Group, a full-service government affairs firm, where I lead the cannabis branch of the firm. Political background : I am a registered Democrat with progressive values. Why are you running for office : I believe in progressive Democratic values and I believe that a diverse set of ideas is helpful to find solutions to the issues we face. Key election issue : Faith in the democratic system and lack of voter participation. Encourage people to exercise their right to vote. Example of a successful project : During the 2017 campaign for Gov. Phil Murphy, campaign, the Latino Outreach team held various Latino policy forums throughout the state. These forums as well as various outreach meetings led to policies later implemented by Gov. Murphy. Those included, New Jersey as a sanctuary state, driver’s licenses for undocumented New Jersey residents, in-state tuition for undocumented immigrants and the $15 minimum wage. Example of a challenge faced : As a person who has been involved behind the scenes in campaigns, both as a volunteer and in a professional role, becoming the candidate and assuming the role, has been a difficult adjustment. As a staffer and consultant for political campaigns, I understand instinctively what needs to be done, as a candidate, it does not always translate. On NJ’s gun laws : I would include childproofing features and no gun purchases after violent offenses. To me these are some of the most basic requirements to include. On the Murphy administration’s climate change proposals : Yes, I absolutely support the administration in making and allowing for these investments to take place. On housing affordability and property taxes : n/a Campaign website

Age : Yes Hometown : Clifton Occupation : Patternmaker Personal background : I attended Lacordaire Academy in Montclair and graduated Pratt Institute in Brooklyn with a B.F.A. in fashion design. Political background : I have been active in New Jersey politics for about five years. I was the Republican nominee for the Assembly special election in the 34th district in 2018 and have been the Republican nominee for Assembly in 2019, 2021 and now in 2023. Why are you running for office : I care deeply about New Jersey and our community. Key election issue : Parents should have a say in their child’s education. I believe that some topics are better dealt with in a family environment . Example of a successful project : My family Example of a challenge faced : Hard work and compromise with lots of care. On NJ’s gun laws : I support our right to self-defense. On the Murphy administration’s climate change proposals : If you want to own an electric car or put solar panels on your roof, I have no issue with that. What I do have a concern for is our government, both at the state and national level, is forcing us to abide by their radical “Green New Deal” plan. It is also concerning to see the amount of marine life that has washed up along our Jersey Shore. I support putting a pause on the offshore wind if it is the main cause of these whale deaths. On housing affordability and property taxes : The cost continues to skyrocket. Every year under the Murphy administration, the state budget continues to increase. The way to solve this problem is by 1) Lowering the budget. 2) Cutting wasteful spending. 3) Lowering property taxes. These three solutions will put more money into the taxpayer’s pocket.

Age : 43 Hometown : Livingston Occupation : School superintendent/principal Personal background : My family’s history of resilience, escaping Nazi persecution as Dutch Jews to find refuge in the Dominican Republic, inspires me. At age 7, my family immigrated to the United States for a better life, settling in Elizabeth, New Jersey. After college, I earned my master’s degree in elementary education and my doctorate in educational leadership at Seton Hall University. Then I earned a second master’s degree in special education at Rutgers. My husband, Ricky Bagolie, is an attorney and together we are blessed with three remarkable sons. Frank, our eldest, is a 17-year-old high school junior, while our twins, Jacob and Aaron, are 14-year-old freshmen. I’ve dedicated my life to education, starting as a public school teacher, advancing to director of special education and principal, and now serving as superintendent/principal of the East Newark public school district. I’m committed to hard work, perseverance and education’s transformative power in our community. Political background : My lifelong journey in Democratic politics began as a student at Elizabeth High School when I dove into the world of grassroots campaigning in Union County, working alongside Sen. Ray Lesniak and Mayor Chris Bollwage. From that moment, my dedication to the Democratic Party’s ideals only deepened, propelling me into the realm of public service. In 2022, I took the bold step of running for Livingston Town Council, emerging victorious in a fiercely contested race. Endorsed over four other exceptionally qualified candidates by the West Essex Tribune, it said, “… her work as a (superintendent), principal and director of special education elsewhere in the state may be similarly valuable. As a certified business administrator, her experience with balancing budgets and writing grants would certainly prove useful. Through public debates and statements, she has shown her knowledge on the issues that affect this town (and those that do not).” Winning this election marked a historic moment as I became the first-ever Latina-Jewish woman to serve on the council and the first woman to do so since 2014. I am now running for Assembly on the Democratic Line in New Jersey’s 27th Legislative District because I see a need for a reasoned voice and diverse perspective, like mine, to actively participate in the process to shape policies and decisions that impact our lives and the lives of future generations. Why are you running for office : I am running for Assembly on the Democratic Line in New Jersey’s 27th Legislative District, representing the communities of Livingston, West Orange, Milburn, Montclair, Roseland and Clifton. I see a need for a thoughtful, diverse and proactive advocate to guide us through the challenges and opportunities we face. My goal is simple: to enhance our community by addressing our shared concerns through legislative action and advocacy, all with the aim of improving people’s lives. As your assemblywoman, I will loudly and proudly champion the fundamental rights of women to make their own health care decisions, free from government interference as women’s rights are under threat like never before. I will advocate for personal choice and equality, support access to education and mental health services, advocate for our seniors, common-sense gun laws, fair labor standards and address climate change, all steps toward creating a more just, equitable and sustainable world. These are crucial topics that have a significant impact on our society’s well being and progress. Key election issue : In this election, New Jersey faces pivotal challenges that demand our attention and action. These key issues include the impending battle for reproductive rights; the pressing need to expand access to quality and affordable health care; the imperative to enhance our education system and provide sufficient funding for our schools while ensuring we have enough educators entering the workforce; the unwavering support for worker rights, public safety and our dedicated first responders and law enforcement personnel; and advocating for the protection of the pensions of our workforce that were promised and earned. Additionally, we must also prioritize job creation, facilitate economic recovery and extend vital support to our small businesses. These issues collectively define the path toward a stronger and more inclusive future for our state. I want to address the important issues raised and share some of the solutions I propose to tackle the key challenges facing our community in this election. First and foremost, I am committed to upholding our cherished Democratic values, especially in the face of adversity. We owe a debt of gratitude to the courageous women’s rights movement that has granted us access to essential health care services, contraception and control over our reproductive choices. This empowerment has propelled women into the workforce, academia and politics. While women’s rights may currently be secure in New Jersey, we cannot take this for granted. Some individuals, including those seeking office in our state, seek to reverse the fertility independence and progress we’ve made. It falls upon our generation to prevent this regression. I staunchly support safeguarding women’s unequivocal right to choose and ensuring that contraception remains affordable and accessible. Additionally, I am a strong advocate for our seniors here in New Jersey. I will work tirelessly to ensure they have access to affordable housing, secure retirement benefits and quality health care. Addressing and reducing gun violence in our communities is another priority, along with preserving open spaces and promoting environmental sustainability. I also stand firmly for love in all its forms, recognizing that all love is love, and I will advocate for equal rights and recognition for all. Our public workers, including law enforcement, first responders and firefighters, deserve our unwavering support, and I am dedicated to providing them with the necessary resources they need to properly perform their jobs and addressing their mental health needs. For working families, I will strengthen workers’ rights, offer job training opportunities and support unions while safeguarding pensions and vehemently opposing any attacks on these hard-earned retirement benefits. Furthermore, I am committed to fostering business growth through infrastructure improvements, responsible regulation streamlining and promoting sound fiscal policies. Finally, as a lifelong teacher, I champion our schools as palaces of learning, for education is the foundation of our nation’s future. It’s not just about classrooms and textbooks; it’s about empowering our young people to dream, innovate, and contribute to society. We must invest in our schools, attract new and support our existing teachers, and ensure that every child, regardless of their background, has the opportunity to receive a quality education. Together, we can protect and advance these fundamental principles that define our great state and pave the way for a brighter future for New Jersey. Example of a successful project : As a councilwoman representing the Township of Livingston, it has been my commitment to address not only local concerns but also to passionately advocate for issues close to my heart, deeply intertwined with the soul of our community. Two recent examples stand out as emblematic of this commitment. First, I took the initiative to encourage my fellow council members to draft and pass a resolution embracing the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s (IHRA) “Working Definition of Antisemitism.” This action was part of our ongoing dedication to condemn and combat anti-Semitism, and all discrimination, both within our community and beyond. Second, drawing from my lifelong passion for reading and experience as an educator, I championed the passage of a resolution affirming “Book Choice Freedom” within our town. This resolution solidified our township’s unwavering support for residents’ freedom to explore a wide range of literary works, firmly denouncing any form of censorship. These actions were unanimously approved and reflect my unwavering commitment to fostering a community that stands against prejudice and values the principles of freedom, education and inclusivity. Example of a challenge faced : My immigrant journey, marked by overcoming poverty, aims to inspire those facing similar challenges. Arriving in a new country filled with hope, my family soon encountered financial hardship, leading to tough choices between rent and food, along with various hardships, like food insecurity, lack of affordable health care and period poverty. Recognizing that education was my escape from poverty, I pursued it relentlessly, even working from age 13. Through hard work and determination, I not only excelled academically but also professionally, breaking free from poverty’s grip and stand as a proud testament to the transformative power of education. Now, I dedicate my life to helping children facing similar struggles, offering them opportunities and guidance to pursue their dreams and break the cycle of poverty. On NJ’s gun laws : I wholeheartedly endorse the enactment of common-sense gun laws that find a middle ground, respecting our Second Amendment rights while addressing crucial public safety issues, considering the significant role of federal regulations in shaping state-level laws. New Jersey’s firearm regulations acknowledge the need for responsible restrictions to enhance community safety. It is of utmost importance that we strive to diminish gun violence while acknowledging the deep-rooted connection between lawful gun ownership and our nation’s history. On the Murphy administration’s climate change proposals : Addressing climate change, Gov. Murphy’s initiatives aim for a greener future but require ongoing review and adjustment to ensure effectiveness. Climate change poses real threats like property damage, agricultural disruption and population displacement, with their associated costs. I support proactive measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, aiming to minimize climate change impacts and protect the environment and residents. Success depends on accessibility and affordability for all, including low-income communities, addressing and funding infrastructure challenges, and fostering collaboration with local businesses, universities, neighboring states and the federal government for a comprehensive regional approach to combat climate change. On housing affordability and property taxes : Effectively addressing New Jersey’s housing challenges, including rent costs, affordability and property taxes, necessitates a comprehensive approach. This involves prioritizing funding for affordable housing programs while minimizing community disruption and empowering local authorities. Strategies encompass subsidies, tax incentives, and partnerships with developers. Additionally, property tax reforms, such as assessment adjustments and tax relief programs, should be explored. Continuous policy evaluation is crucial, including a review of Fair Share Housing policies, aiming for equitable solutions that benefit municipalities and affordable housing advocates. Transparent guidelines, financial incentives, streamlined approval processes and adaptive reuse of existing structures can contribute to a more inclusive housing landscape while involving residents in decision-making to align policies with community needs. Final thoughts: I am honored to stand alongside my running mates, John McKeon for Senate and Alixon Collazos-Gill for Assembly. I am deeply grateful for the opportunity to be a part of this team, and together, in Trenton, we will ensure that the 27th District receives the strong voice it rightfully deserves. Campaign website

answers.Personal background: I am a lifelong Essex County resident, born in Montclair where I attended public schools through high school graduation. answers.Political background: I have been involved in political campaigns at the national, state, county and local level for more than 30 years. For more than two decades, I have served as a district leader on the Maplewood County Committee and as vice chair for more than 10 years.
answers.Why are you running for office?: I was asked to run for the open Assembly seat vacated by my great friend and mentor Assemblywoman Mila Jasey following a robust discussion as to which candidate among those under consideration would best represent the newly drawn 28th Legislative District. The 28th consists of five communities, including two wealthy, racially diverse towns (South Orange and Maplewood) and three (Irvington, Hillside and parts of Newark), that face persistent socioeconomic challenges. Representing diverse suburban and urban districts, with what will be at times very different priorities and concerns, will not be an easy task, but my knowledge, experience and skill set will enable me to be an effective advocate for the entire district.
answers.Key election issue: Ensuring individuals and families have safe, affordable places to call home, with access to employment opportunities and job training and re-training to enhance their earning potential, and the ability to attend schools where the quality of education is not ZIP-code dependent.
answers.Example of a successful project: I am proud of the work that I have done in my capacity as deputy Essex County clerk to promote the vote by mail and the early voting efforts. Safe and secure elections are critical, and the processes that we have implemented in the County Clerk’s Office working with our Clerk Chris Durkin have ensured that vote-by-mail ballots are received by voters requesting them, publicizing the availability and locations of drop boxes and the dates and locations of early voting.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: The greatest challenge we face is maintaining voter confidence in the election process. We have committed to ensuring that every vote will be counted, and it is a tremendous responsibility at a time when so many voters believe that the process is tainted and votes are suppressed. The work we do, in concert with the Board of Elections, ensures that the Essex County voting process is secure, accessible and a paper trail exists of every vote cast, whether by vote by mail or at our hundreds of polling locations.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: New Jersey’s gun laws are among the strongest in the nation, and I would have voted in favor of every single bill that has helped secure that reputation. Concealed carry is dangerous and not in the best interest of our communities, individually or collectively, and I do not believe that our definitions of sensitive places where guns should be banned is overbroad. If elected, I will support reasonable regulations to stop the scourge of gun violence, including banning ghost guns, stringent background checks, raising the age of purchase and possession of a firearm to age 21 and would support mandatory training in the use of firearms and securing them when they are not in use. I also support restrictions on permissible purchase to promote lawful use only.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: Just as is the case nationwide, New Jersey has an overreliance on fossil fuel that must be addressed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. If we continue to focus our efforts upon expansion of wind and solar energy use, while also building with green products, incentivize the purchase of hybrid and (preferably) electric vehicles, and provide adequate charging stations to meet the expanding need, the market will be able to end fossil fuel use by 2035. Alternatively, climate change will continue to exacerbate to a point where we may well find ourselves unable to reverse the man-made damage to the environment we have created.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: Implementation of a statewide rent control policy, continuing to work with agencies, such as HCDNNJ and FSNJ, to build affordable housing, renovate existing buildings to meet the need by incentivizing community development, expand HMFA home ownership financial programs, use statutory tools that have been created to prevent foreclosures, continue to expand eligibility for ANCHOR, senior freeze and carefully monitor the initiation of StayNJ in 2026 in the hope that we have found a real solutions to enabling our seniors to age in place by providing meaningful tax relief.

And we need to do even more on climate change adaptation to assist communities in navigating the strong impacts of a warming planet, such as more intense storms and days of extreme heat, that are already very much with us today.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: As an assemblyman, I will work to ease barriers to building new housing, including taking a hard look at restrictive zoning that prevents affordable options and greater density, as well as working to boost state incentives for affordable housing. I also back greater state funding for education, which would relieve upward pressure on property taxes.

answers.Personal background: Hometown is Union City. Graduated from Emerson High School. Has experience in multiple levels of government from local to state. He is the longest-running mayor of Union City, now serving his 23rd year. He was elected as state senator for the 33rd Legislative District and is currently serving his 15th year.
answers.Political background: Was first elected mayor of Union City in 2000. He served on the Hudson County Board of Chosen Freeholders from 1998 to 2004. Elected to the General Assembly from 2004 to 2007. He then ran for Senate and has been representing the 33rd Legislative District from 2008 to the present. He is chair of the Judiciary Committee and vice chair of Community and Urban Affairs.
answers.Why are you running for office?: Senator Stack has a passion for constituent services and helping those residents in his district.

answers.Personal background: Joseph Belnome is a dedicated and accomplished individual hailing from Newark, New Jersey, and raised in the neighboring town of Belleville. He has built a remarkable life rooted in his strong work ethic, community engagement and commitment to public service. Born to parents who hailed from the same town in Sicily, Joseph witnessed firsthand their journey to American citizenship upon immigrating to the United States. In his earlier years, Joseph honed his skills as a journeyman bricklayer in Local #4, where his craftsmanship and attention to detail were highly regarded. With a deep passion for construction and ensuring the safety of buildings, Joseph transitioned his career and now serves as an inspector in the Building Department of Belleville Township. Through this role, he plays a vital part in upholding safety standards and ensuring the compliance of structures, fostering a secure environment for residents and businesses alike. Joseph’s dedication to public service extends beyond his professional endeavors. As a district leader for the Belleville Republican Party, he plays a pivotal role in shaping local politics and advocating for the principles and values he holds dear. He has actively contributed his time and expertise to various mayoral and Board of Education campaigns, striving to effect positive change and improve the quality of life for the community he calls home.
answers.Political background: District leader for Belleville Republican Party.
answers.Why are you running for office?: We are a nation in decline. Radical left policies, such as open borders, are straining public services and creating a booming enterprise for cartels to traffic women and children. Our state is allowing the sexualization of children as young as kindergarten by exposing them to sexually explicit books in our libraries and insisting on talking to children about their gender. What I’ve witnessed from the pandemic in this state can only be described as tyranny. Using nonsensical solutions with unproven methods, such as masks and social distancing, in addition to basic mandates of newly created experimental vaccines at the same time opening our election to fraud with ballot boxes and mandatory mail-in ballots – I’ve had enough.
answers.Key election issue: Parental rights. Specifically I’m fighting to stop the state from keeping secrets from parents about their children in regards to changing their gender.
answers.Example of a successful project: As vice president of a civic association, we successfully repurposed pallets into planters and placed them around our community.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: It’s challenging living in tyranny. With perseverance and prayer for new leadership and now running for office to make a difference, I shall overcome.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: The Second Amendment shall not be infringed. New Jersey gun laws are way too strict and have done nothing to reduce any crimes. They only affect and restrict law-abiding legal gun owners.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: I would never allow a moratorium to not pay rent while homeowners still need to pay their mortgages. I am open to restricting corporations from buying residential homes in our communities. This would make sure corporations don’t manipulate the housing markets and reduce the cost of housing and rents.

answers.Personal background: Born and raised in Montclair, senior pastor for 34 years of the New Calvary Baptist Church of Newark, New Jersey. Graduate of Northern Baptist School of Religion, executive food sales for Acme Institutional, serving schools and corporate cafeterias in the northern New Jersey area. I am northeast director for LEARN, the Life Education and Resource Network, educating the African American community on health and productive lifestyle choices. I was awarded the NAACP community service award and lifetime achievement award by LEARN. Married to Regina. We have four children and live in East Orange.
answers.Political background: I have been engaged in politics since 2005 and have run as a Democrat, Independant and ran for Congress 2021.
answers.Why are you running for office?: To create a change in Trenton and represent the citizens and their rights in government.
answers.Key election issue: Parental rights.
answers.Example of a successful project: Creating a social activism organization, LEARN Northeast Community Organizers.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: Creating a productive working environment for youth and seniors. We found open forums and home visitation brought about like-minded projects or ideas that were common ground desires.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: I would not change laws until the present ones are fully enforced.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: This nation has the resources to be self-sustaining and all sources should be pursued.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: Rent control and raising the percentage of affordable housing units created in building projects.

answers.Personal background: It has been my honor to be a husband, father, coach and brother of Omega Psi Phi Fraternity Inc. Each of these duties has shaped my career, passion for activism, legislation, engagement with residents and my perspective on the importance of community as an Assemblyman. You can’t spell Benjie without NJ.
answers.Political background: I have had both the pleasure and support to serve the community as an elected official since 2012. I have been excited to collaborate with residents and colleagues to create opportunities that make New Jersey a more affordable place to live, build a strong educational infrastructure for public and charter school students to learn and establish programs that assist seniors with health care and housing.
answers.Why are you running for office?: I am running for office because I believe that it is my social responsibility to continue to lead and learn about the pockets of our community that need access to support. My faith, family and neighbors are all anchors of support for me and I’d like to continue to provide that care for our community.
answers.Key election issue: A key issue in this election is housing; despite all the accomplishments that we’ve made with programs like senior freeze; we’ve still got a long way to go in evaluating how this service can be the catalyst for change and create others like it.
answers.Example of a successful project: I’ve partnered to do so many it’s difficult to choose; one of my most proud titles is being a father coach and mentor to so many young Black and Hispanic youth. I love being a positive demonstration in their life. On another note, I am on the Budget Committee and I think participating in how the annual budget is distributed is critical to the trajectory of our state and I am always so proud to support the people and programs through my vote.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: There are so many people in New Jersey that still need assistance; whether they do or do not meet legal criteria people experience hardship. Gripping the reality that for one administration we may not be able to get to everyone is tough and unsettling but it’s important that we put our best effort forward to reach as many and provide quality care as soon as we are able.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: I think gun violence is a prevalent issue in our nation. I think that restrictions need to be in place to ensure that minors have no access to firearms, the licensed carriers take the most precaution, that we are emphasizing health and well-being intervention methods and also educating our youth and adults about the danger of firearms.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: Yes, protecting our environment is critical to having a safe state for our communities to thrive.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: I’m proud that this past budget set record investments into housing affordability programs, tax relief, public school education and higher education. This investment will give people an opportunity to both live and continue their education.
answers.Final thoughts: Thank you for reviewing my answers! You can’t spell Benjie without NJ.

answers.Personal background: 23 years U.S. Army with two combat deployments in Iraq, retired Jersey City firefighter, B.A. in business management, B.A. in emergency management and master’s degree in emergency management.
answers.Political background: I have never held political office.
answers.Why are you running for office?: Because I don’t believe I’m being represented. I believe in consent of the governed and I no longer consent.
answers.Key election issue: Parental rights.
answers.Example of a successful project: I’ve helped many times to put together events at my Amvets and American Legion.
answers.Example of a challenge faced: Military service and my strength to overcome it is through my faith in Jesus.
answers.On NJ’s gun laws: I would ensure that if someone is arrested with an illegal firearm that they are actually prosecuted and not released without bail.
answers.On the Murphy administration’s climate c: I do not support his initiatives because consensus of the population has never been given on whether this is the appropriate way to approach these expenditures and new mandates. These projects and mandates were done unilaterally by the executive. With all expenditures and mandates these should be done by legislation.
answers.On housing affordability and property ta: The first step is reigning in budgets that have over $1 billion in earmarks that are only used to try to buy votes. We have so many new developments that are being built that the going rents in the new construction have exorbitant rates, which increase the fair market value of existing rents. Lowering property taxes can be done by changing the school aid formula that treats most of the cities in my district as affluent when in fact they are blue-collar and middle-class areas. There are cities that have 2,700 citizens that get the same school aid as my city of 22,000. I would demand that be changed.
